steps.title: Look at the blank and what comes before it.
steps.content: The blank comes after the word 'need'. We need to figure out how 'need' connects to the action of 'digesting their food'.

steps.title: Consider how 'need' works with other verbs.
steps.content: When you 'need' to do something, you typically use 'to' followed by the base form of the verb (like 'to eat', 'to sleep', 'to study'). This structure shows the purpose or goal of the 'need'.

steps.title: Choose the option that fits the 'need to' structure.
steps.content: Since the reindeer 'need' to perform the action of digesting their food, the correct way to express this is 'need to digest'.

19f079e1-4d95-4357-a687-24d2a4e98fbf.key_insight: When you use the verb 'need' to talk about an action someone has to do, you almost always follow it with 'to' and the base form of the verb (e.g., 'need to go', 'need to understand').

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Just saying 'need digest' doesn't sound right in English. 'Digest' on its own doesn't connect properly to 'need' in this way.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: 'Will digest' talks about something that will happen in the future, but it doesn't fit with 'need' to show what the reindeer are required to do. You wouldn't say 'they need will digest'.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: While 'digesting' is a verb form, 'need digesting' usually means something *else* needs to digest *it*, not that the reindeer need to do the digesting themselves. For example, 'The food needs digesting' means the food needs to be digested by someone or something.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what kind of words or punctuation come right before and after it. The blank comes after the word "advance" and before the phrase "its predictions are therefore more short-term."

highlights.text: its predictions are therefore more short-term

steps.title: Check the first part of the sentence
steps.content: Now, let's read the part of the sentence *before* the blank: "A subseasonal weather forecast attempts to predict weather conditions three to four weeks in advance." Can this stand alone as a complete thought? Yes, it can. It has a subject ("A subseasonal weather forecast") and a verb ("attempts to predict") and expresses a full idea.

steps.title: Check the second part of the sentence
steps.content: Next, let's read the part of the sentence *after* the blank: "its predictions are therefore more short-term than those of the seasonal forecast, which attempts to predict the weather more than a month in advance." Can this stand alone as a complete thought? Yes, it can. It has a subject ("its predictions") and a verb ("are") and expresses a full idea.

highlights.text: its predictions are therefore more short-term than those of the seasonal forecast, which attempts to predict the weather more than a month in advance

steps.title: Connect two complete thoughts
steps.content: Since both parts of the sentence are complete thoughts, we need a strong way to connect them. A semicolon (;) is perfect for joining two complete thoughts that are closely related in meaning. It's stronger than a comma but not as strong as a period.

1b1796a9-9cbf-450d-bb09-476787da6797.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts (sentences) that are closely related, you can join them with a semicolon. A single comma is not strong enough to connect two complete thoughts on its own.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using just a comma here creates a run-on sentence. You can't connect two complete thoughts with only a comma; it's like trying to stop a train with a feather.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Putting no punctuation at all between two complete thoughts creates a run-on sentence. The two thoughts just crash into each other without a proper break.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using "and" by itself isn't enough to connect two complete thoughts. To use "and" correctly, you would need a comma *before* it (e.g., "advance, and its predictions..."). Without the comma, it's still a run-on.

steps.title: Find the main subject of the sentence
steps.content: First, let's figure out what the sentence is really about. The blank needs a verb, so we need to find the noun that is performing the action or being described. Read the sentence and identify the core subject before the blank. Don't get distracted by the long list of examples in the middle!

highlights.text: ranging from the Kikkoman soy sauce bottle to the Yamaha VMAX motorcycle to the Komachi bullet train

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Once you've found the main subject, check if it's singular (one thing) or plural (more than one thing). Our subject is 'Objects,' which clearly ends with an 's,' telling us it's plural.

steps.title: Match the verb to the plural subject
steps.content: Now that we know the subject 'Objects' is plural, we need a plural verb to agree with it. Look at the answer choices and pick the verb that works with a plural subject.

1c4c5335-5d57-496e-9baf-dad9988dceaf.key_insight: Always make sure your verb agrees with its subject. If the subject is plural, the verb must be plural. Don't let extra words between the subject and verb trick you!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'was' is singular, but the subject 'Objects' is plural. This creates a mismatch.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'is' is singular, but the subject 'Objects' is plural. The sentence needs a plural verb.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The verb phrase 'has been' is singular. Since the subject 'Objects' is plural, 'has been' doesn't fit.

steps.title: Find the blank and look at what comes before and after it.
steps.content: The blank is right after the word "estimates". Before the blank, we have a phrase in parentheses: "(as many as 200,000, by some estimates". This whole phrase is extra information that could be removed without changing the main meaning of the sentence.

steps.title: Check for matching punctuation.
steps.content: When you open a parenthetical phrase with an opening parenthesis (like the one before "as many as"), you need to close it with a matching closing parenthesis. The blank is exactly where that closing parenthesis should go.

steps.title: Choose the correct punctuation.
steps.content: Since the phrase started with an opening parenthesis, it must end with a closing parenthesis. No other punctuation is needed immediately after the closing parenthesis because the sentence continues smoothly with "in a complex of comfortable apartments...".

highlights.text: in a complex of comfortable apartments

2b32b6b5-8123-44f6-bc14-86fb78e28d42.key_insight: If you open a parenthetical phrase with a parenthesis, you must close it with a parenthesis. Think of parentheses like bookends!

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice adds an unnecessary comma after the closing parenthesis. The phrase 'in a complex...' flows directly from the main part of the sentence without needing a comma to separate it.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: You can't mix and match punctuation like this. If you start a parenthetical phrase with a parenthesis, you can't end it with a dash. They don't go together.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice leaves the parenthetical phrase open, which is a grammatical error. Every opening parenthesis needs a closing one.

steps.title: Identify the core sentence
steps.content: First, let's find the main part of the sentence without the blank. It reads: "Eli Eisenberg, a genetics expert at Tel Aviv University in Israel, recently discovered that ______ have a special genetic ability called RNA editing that confers evolutionary advantages." The blank needs to introduce the subject of what was discovered.

highlights.text: Eli Eisenberg, a genetics expert at Tel Aviv University in Israel, recently discovered that
have a special genetic ability called RNA editing that confers evolutionary advantages.

steps.title: Look for extra information
steps.content: The blank contains the word "cephalopods," which is the subject. The rest of the information in the blank, "ocean dwellers that include the squid, the octopus, and the cuttlefish," is extra information that describes cephalopods. This kind of extra information needs to be set off by punctuation.

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation for extra information
steps.content: When you have extra information that could be removed without changing the main meaning of the sentence, you can set it off with a pair of commas, a pair of parentheses, or a pair of dashes. Dashes are often used for emphasis or when the extra information itself contains commas (like a list). Here, the description of cephalopods includes a list of animals, so dashes work well to clearly separate the entire descriptive phrase.

highlights.text: ocean dwellers that include the squid , the octopus , and the cuttlefish

2c89c59a-b995-45ac-b8fc-fe0d1f93a13e.key_insight: If you have a chunk of extra information that could be removed from a sentence without breaking it, you need to set it off with a pair of matching punctuation marks: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'cephalopods' but doesn't have a closing punctuation mark after 'cuttlefish' to properly set off the descriptive phrase. It leaves the sentence grammatically incomplete because the extra information isn't fully separated.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with a dash after 'cephalopods' and closes with a dash after 'dwellers,' but then it adds a comma after 'cuttlefish.' This mixes punctuation marks incorrectly and doesn't fully enclose the entire descriptive phrase 'ocean dwellers that include the squid, the octopus, and the cuttlefish' within a consistent pair of punctuation marks.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'cephalopods' but then uses a colon after 'include.' A colon usually introduces a list or an explanation that follows directly, but here it's trying to be part of an introductory phrase that needs to be set off. It also ends with a comma after 'cuttlefish,' which doesn't properly close the introductory phrase that started with a comma.

steps.title: Look at the blank and the surrounding words
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence leading up to the blank: "Psychophysicist Howard Moskowitz was hired by a soda company to determine how much artificial sweetener ______." The sentence starts by telling us what Moskowitz was hired to do.

highlights.text: Psychophysicist Howard Moskowitz was hired by a soda company to determine how much artificial sweetener

steps.title: Check if it's a question or a statement
steps.content: The key here is whether the sentence is asking a direct question or making a statement about what Moskowitz was trying to figure out. The phrase "to determine how much artificial sweetener..." indicates that the sentence is describing the *goal* of his work, not asking a question directly to the reader. It's a statement about what he was trying to find out.

highlights.text: to determine how much artificial sweetener

steps.title: Choose the correct phrasing and punctuation
steps.content: Since the sentence is a statement, not a question, it should end with a period. Also, the phrasing "how much artificial sweetener most people prefer" is correct for an embedded question (a question that's part of a larger statement). Adding "do" (as in "do most people prefer") would make it sound like a direct question, which doesn't fit here.

highlights.text: most people prefer in a diet drink.
do most people prefer in a diet drink?

31c57dfe-c1ae-42e4-a19c-087dee62781b.key_insight: When a question is embedded within a larger statement (like 'He wanted to know how much...'), it usually doesn't need a question mark and often drops the 'do/does/did' helper verb.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a question mark, but the sentence is a statement about what Moskowitz was trying to determine, not a direct question. The word 'do' also makes it sound like a direct question, which is incorrect for an embedded question.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a period, which is good, but it still includes 'do.' The sentence already has the main verb 'was hired to determine,' so adding 'do' here makes the sentence clunky and grammatically incorrect for an embedded question.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses the correct phrasing ('most people prefer') but ends with a question mark. Since the sentence is a statement describing Moskowitz's goal, it should end with a period, not a question mark.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence carefully, paying close attention to the blank and the words immediately before and after it. We have "pages ______ a collection of Norse tales." The word "from" is meant to connect "pages" to "a collection of Norse tales," telling us where the pages came from.

steps.title: Identify the role of 'from'
steps.content: The word "from" acts as a preposition here, starting a phrase that describes the pages. It tells us the origin of the pages. When a preposition introduces a phrase that is essential to the meaning of the sentence, you usually don't need any punctuation right after the preposition.

steps.title: Check for unnecessary punctuation
steps.content: In this sentence, "from a collection of Norse tales" directly tells us what kind of pages were discovered. It's not extra information that could be removed without changing the core meaning. Therefore, no punctuation (like a colon, comma, or dash) is needed between "from" and the rest of its phrase.

33120da7-30bd-4823-9b41-f807fb25b144.key_insight: When a preposition (like 'from,' 'in,' 'on,' 'at') introduces a phrase that is essential to the meaning of the sentence, don't put punctuation between the preposition and the rest of its phrase.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using a colon after 'from' is incorrect. A colon usually introduces a list or an explanation, and it should follow a complete thought. Here, 'pages from' is not a complete thought, and the colon illogically separates 'from' from the phrase it introduces.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Putting a comma after 'from' incorrectly breaks up the prepositional phrase. The phrase 'from a collection of Norse tales' is essential to describe the pages, and a comma would create an awkward and grammatically incorrect pause.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using a dash after 'from' is similar to using a comma or colon here – it incorrectly separates the preposition from the phrase it introduces. Dashes are used for emphasis or to set off non-essential information, neither of which applies here.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence with the blank: "As Spivak points out, Saville is not the protagonist of Shelley’s ______ as the recipient of the letters that frame the book’s narrative, she’s the 'occasion' of it." We need to figure out how to connect "Saville is not the protagonist of Shelley's novel" with "as the recipient of the letters that frame the book's narrative, she's the 'occasion' of it."

steps.title: Check if each side is a complete thought
steps.content: Let's break down the sentence. Is "Saville is not the protagonist of Shelley's novel" a complete thought? Yes, it has a subject (Saville) and a verb (is) and expresses a full idea. Is "as the recipient of the letters that frame the book's narrative, she's the 'occasion' of it" a complete thought? Yes, it also has a subject (she) and a verb (is) and expresses a full idea. Since both sides are complete thoughts, we need strong punctuation to connect them.

steps.title: Choose the right connector
steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts, you can connect them with a period (making two separate sentences), a semicolon, or a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (like 'and,' 'but,' 'or'). Here, the second complete thought starts with 'rather,' which acts like a connecting word. A semicolon before 'rather' is perfect for joining two complete thoughts, especially when 'rather' introduces a contrasting idea.

3a75694a-5b45-474d-8979-0ae53b3abcd7.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts that could stand alone as sentences, you need a strong connector like a period, a semicolon, or a comma with a coordinating conjunction (like 'and,' 'but,' 'or'). A comma alone isn't strong enough!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Putting just 'novel' here creates a run-on sentence. You'd have two complete thoughts smashed together without any punctuation or connecting word, which makes it hard to read and grammatically incorrect.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using just a comma after 'novel' creates a comma splice. A comma by itself isn't strong enough to join two complete thoughts. It's like trying to hold two big train cars together with a tiny string – it won't work!

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice also creates a comma splice. Even with 'rather' following the comma, a single comma isn't enough to connect two complete thoughts. You need a semicolon before 'rather' or a comma and a coordinating conjunction if 'rather' wasn't there.

steps.title: Find the main subject of the sentence
steps.content:
First, let's figure out what the sentence is really about. The blank needs a verb, so we need to find the noun that performs the action (or is described by) that verb. Read the sentence carefully: "The village of Panduyacu in Ecuador ______ one of the rare places in the world located almost directly on the equator."

The main thing we're talking about here is "The village." The phrase "of Panduyacu in Ecuador" just tells us more about which village.

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Now that we know the subject is "village," we need to decide if it's singular (one) or plural (more than one). "Village" is clearly singular.

steps.title: Match the verb to the singular subject
steps.content:
Since our subject, "village," is singular, we need a singular verb to match it. Let's look at the choices:

*   A: "are being" is plural.
*   B: "have been" is plural.
*   C: "is" is singular.
*   D: "are" is plural.

The only singular verb that matches our singular subject "village" is "is."

3edf8ed8-0ba6-4fa4-896d-0e6677d04e9f.key_insight: Always make sure your verb agrees with its subject. If the subject is singular, the verb must be singular. If the subject is plural, the verb must be plural. Don't get tricked by words or phrases that come between the subject and the verb!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: The verb "are being" is plural, but the subject "village" is singular. This creates a mismatch in number, making the sentence grammatically incorrect.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The verb "have been" is plural, but the subject "village" is singular. This choice doesn't match the number of the subject.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The verb "are" is plural, but the subject "village" is singular. This is a common mistake; remember to match the verb to the main subject, not to any words in a modifying phrase.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence up to the blank: "Before the park’s construction, the surface temperature 30 meters outside of the park boundary was 0.1°C cooler than that of a control area." Now, read what comes immediately after the blank: "construction, the temperature 30 meters outside of the boundary was 1.7°C cooler than that of the control area."

steps.title: Check if each side is a complete thought
steps.content: The part before the blank, "Before the park’s construction, the surface temperature 30 meters outside of the park boundary was 0.1°C cooler than that of a control area," is a complete thought. It has a subject (temperature) and a verb (was) and makes sense on its own. The part after the blank, starting with "After construction, the temperature 30 meters outside of the boundary was 1.7°C cooler than that of the control area," is also a complete thought. It also has a subject (temperature) and a verb (was) and makes sense on its own.

steps.title: Connect two complete thoughts correctly
steps.content: Since both sides of the blank are complete thoughts, you need strong punctuation to separate them. A period is perfect for this, as it signals the end of one sentence and the start of another. The word "After" then correctly begins the new sentence, indicating a change in time.

3ef575da-a80d-4b8e-a9cb-5b5ab01fdc25.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts, you need strong punctuation like a period or a semicolon to separate them. A comma alone isn't strong enough.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice creates a run-on sentence. It jams two complete thoughts together without any punctuation to separate them, making it hard to read and understand where one idea ends and the next begins.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice also creates a run-on sentence. A comma by itself isn't strong enough to separate two complete thoughts. It's like trying to stop a car with a feather instead of a brake. Plus, there's no need for a comma between 'after' and 'construction'.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice creates a comma splice. You can't use just a comma to connect two complete thoughts. It's a common mistake that makes the sentence grammatically incorrect and confusing.

steps.title: Find the blank and identify the action
steps.content: First, look at the blank. The sentence after the blank says "______ created additional installations using a variety of sweets." We need to figure out who or what "created" these installations.

steps.title: Look for the subject of the action
steps.content: Now, read the sentences before the blank to find out who is doing the creating. The first sentence introduces "Félix González-Torres" as the artist who debuted the sculpture. The second sentence talks about "González-Torres" becoming known for using candy.

steps.title: Match the pronoun to the subject
steps.content: Since Félix González-Torres is a single person, we need a singular pronoun to refer to him. The word that fits best is "He."

40e1c303-b777-4241-8166-650e534cfd62.key_insight: When you see a blank that needs a pronoun, always look for the person or thing the pronoun is replacing. Make sure the pronoun (like 'he,' 'she,' 'it,' 'they') matches that person or thing in number (singular or plural).

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using 'They all' would mean multiple people created the installations, but the text only mentions one artist, Félix González-Torres.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: 'Those' is a plural word, but we're talking about a single artist, Félix González-Torres. It also doesn't clearly refer to a person.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: 'Both' means two things or people, but the passage only discusses one artist, Félix González-Torres. There isn't a second person or thing for 'both' to refer to.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's find the blank. It's right after the word "taxation." Now, let's read the sentence carefully, paying attention to what comes before and after the phrase "through trade and centralized taxation."

steps.title: Identify the extra information
steps.content: The phrase "through trade and centralized taxation" tells us *how* the economic system funded projects. This information is extra; the sentence would still make sense without it. Notice that there's already a comma after "that" (that, through trade...). This suggests that the phrase "through trade and centralized taxation" is set off by commas as extra information.

steps.title: Use matching punctuation for extra information
steps.content: When you have extra information in the middle of a sentence, it's usually set off by a pair of commas. Since there's already a comma before "through trade and centralized taxation," we need a matching comma after "taxation" to complete the pair. This shows that the phrase is a non-essential detail.

4726821c-de5f-4694-ab33-3b1a0ac5f33e.key_insight: If a phrase in the middle of a sentence is just extra information (the sentence still makes sense without it), set it off with a pair of commas.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: A colon introduces a list or an explanation, and it doesn't pair with a comma to set off extra information in this way. Using a colon here would create an awkward break in the sentence.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: A dash can set off extra information, but it usually pairs with another dash, not a comma. Using a dash with a comma creates mismatched punctuation and makes the sentence confusing.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Without any punctuation after "taxation," the phrase "through trade and centralized taxation" isn't properly set off as extra information. This makes the sentence harder to read and grammatically incorrect because the introductory comma after 'that' is left hanging without a closing comma.

steps.title: Identify the introductory phrase and the blank
steps.content: First, look at the beginning of the sentence. We have an introductory phrase: "Named in 1999 as one of the greatest achievements by a US chemist in the past hundred years." This phrase describes something that was named an achievement. The blank comes right after this phrase.

highlights.text: Named in 1999 as one of the greatest achievements by a US chemist in the past hundred years,

steps.title: Determine what the introductory phrase describes
steps.content: The introductory phrase describes an 'achievement.' We need to make sure that whatever comes right after the comma is the actual 'achievement' being described. What was named one of the greatest achievements? Not Percy Julian himself, not the year 1935, and not just the chemical. It was Julian's *synthesis* (the act of creating it) of the chemical that was the achievement.

highlights.text: Named in 1999 as one of the greatest achievements by a US chemist in the past hundred years,

steps.title: Match the subject to the description
steps.content: The subject immediately following the comma must be what the introductory phrase is describing. Choice C correctly places "Julian's 1935 synthesis of the alkaloid physostigmine" right after the comma. This makes it clear that the *synthesis* (the achievement) was named in 1999.

4733b0f3-7f3a-40c1-b43f-e01ec99ea821.key_insight: When a descriptive phrase starts a sentence, the word or phrase immediately following the comma must be the thing being described. This is called a modifier, and it needs to clearly modify the subject that follows it.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice says, "Named...years, Julian synthesized..." This incorrectly suggests that Julian himself was named one of the greatest achievements, rather than his work or discovery.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice says, "Named...years, in 1935 Julian synthesized..." This incorrectly suggests that the year '1935' was named one of the greatest achievements, which doesn't make sense.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice says, "Named...years, the alkaloid physostigmine was synthesized..." This incorrectly suggests that the chemical itself was named one of the greatest achievements, rather than the *act* of synthesizing it.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's look at the blank. Before it, we have the word "themes." After it, we have "healing, self-discovery, and memory." These words describe what kind of themes Pindell explored.

steps.title: Connect the ideas smoothly
steps.content: We need a word that connects "themes" to the list of specific themes that follows. The word "of" is perfect for this because it shows possession or relationship, indicating that the themes *are* healing, self-discovery, and memory.

steps.title: Avoid unnecessary punctuation
steps.content: When a preposition like "of" directly introduces its object (in this case, the list "healing, self-discovery, and memory"), you generally don't need any punctuation between them. Adding a comma, dash, or colon would create an awkward pause where none is needed.

48ee7f45-4a7d-4fcb-9b74-f3812bcb37d7.key_insight: Don't add punctuation between a preposition (like 'of') and the words it directly introduces, unless there's a very specific reason like an interruption.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Adding a comma after 'of' creates an unnecessary pause and breaks the direct connection between the preposition and its object. It makes the sentence sound choppy.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: A dash after 'of' is usually used for a sudden break in thought or to emphasize something. Here, the list of themes directly follows 'of' without any break, so a dash is out of place.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: A colon after 'of' would imply that a list or explanation is coming, which is true, but 'of' already serves that connecting purpose. Using both 'of' and a colon is redundant and grammatically incorrect in this context.

steps.title: Find the subject of the verb
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what word needs a verb. The blank is for a verb, and we need to figure out what noun or pronoun is doing the action. Look at the phrase right before the blank: "each one of these plays, which include Henry V and Richard III." The key part here is "each one."

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: The phrase "each one" tells us we're talking about *one* play at a time, individually. Even though it's followed by "of these plays," the word "each" makes the subject singular. Think of it like saying "every single one."

steps.title: Match the verb to the singular subject
steps.content: Since our subject, "each one," is singular, the verb also needs to be singular. In the present tense, singular verbs often end in "-s." Let's look at the choices. "Focuses" is the singular form of the verb. The sentence is talking about a general truth, so the present tense is appropriate.

4acb42dd-d12f-45ec-a0e5-b1695f294f49.key_insight: When you see 'each one,' 'every one,' or 'one of' followed by a plural noun, the subject is almost always singular. The verb needs to match that singular subject.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'focus' is plural. It would be correct if the subject were plural (e.g., 'The plays focus'), but 'each one' is singular.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'are focused' is plural. It also uses a passive voice construction ('are focused on') which isn't necessary here; the plays actively 'focus' on a figure.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'were focused' is plural and past tense. The subject 'each one' is singular, and the sentence describes a general characteristic of the plays, so present tense is needed, not past tense.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what comes right before and after it. The blank is after "California" and before "received."

steps.title: Identify the subject and verb
steps.content: In this sentence, "the Huntington Library in California" is the subject, and "received" is the main verb. The subject tells us *who* or *what* is doing the action, and the verb tells us *what* action they are doing.

steps.title: Connect the subject directly to its verb
steps.content: In standard English, you generally don't put punctuation directly between a subject and its main verb. The subject "the Huntington Library in California" needs to flow directly into its verb "received" without interruption. Adding a comma, colon, or dash would incorrectly separate them.

steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts, you can't just put them next to each other (that's a run-on sentence) or connect them with only a comma (that's a comma splice).
