why_wrong.reason: Using 'will have gone' puts the action in the future perfect tense, which doesn't match the present tense of 'appears' and 'symbolizes.' It makes it sound like the tortoise's naming will be completed at some future point, which doesn't fit the context of describing the play.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using 'went' puts the action in the simple past tense. This clashes with the present tense verbs 'appears' and 'symbolizes,' making the sentence jump between timeframes unnecessarily. We're describing the play's current state, not a past event.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using 'had gone' puts the action in the past perfect tense, which indicates an action completed before another past action. This doesn't fit because the other verbs ('appears,' 'symbolizes') are in the present tense, and we're describing an ongoing characteristic of the tortoise in the play.

steps.title: Look for time clues in the sentence
steps.content: The first step in verb tense questions is to find any words or phrases that tell you *when* something happened or is happening. In this sentence, pay close attention to the phrase at the end.

steps.title: Understand what the time clue means
steps.content: The phrase "since it began in 2012" tells us two important things: the action started in the past (2012) and it has continued up to the present moment. We need a verb tense that shows an action that began in the past and is still ongoing or has an effect on the present.

steps.title: Choose the verb tense that fits
steps.content: The present perfect tense (have/has + past participle) is used for actions that started in the past and continue into the present, or actions completed in the past that are relevant now. Since the volunteers started contributing in 2012 and are still part of the project, 'have contributed' is the correct choice.

fa0f023a-a63a-4cd3-bc50-5f433cdf5bb7.key_insight: When you see 'since' followed by a past date or event, you usually need the present perfect tense (have/has + past participle) because it shows an action that started then and continues to now.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'contribute,' it sounds like they contribute regularly right now, but it doesn't connect that action back to when the project started in 2012. It misses the 'since 2012' part.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'will contribute,' it means they haven't contributed yet but will in the future. This doesn't make sense with 'since it began in 2012,' which tells us their contributions started in the past.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'will be contributing,' it also refers to an action that will happen in the future. This doesn't fit the phrase 'since it began in 2012,' which clearly indicates that the contributions started in the past and are ongoing.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what comes right before and after it. The blank is after "1150" and before "it one of the largest cities in North America at the time."

highlights.text: it one of the largest cities in North America at the time.

steps.title: Check if the parts are complete thoughts
steps.content: Now, let's read the sentence up to the blank: "Archaeologists have estimated that the pre-Columbian Native American city of Cahokia, located across the Mississippi River from modern-day St. Louis, Missouri, had as many as 20,000 inhabitants in the year 1150 CE." This is a complete thought. Next, let's look at the part after the blank: "making it one of the largest cities in North America at the time." This phrase describes the previous statement but isn't a complete thought on its own because it doesn't have its own subject performing the action.

steps.title: Connect a complete thought to an incomplete one
steps.content: When you have a complete thought followed by an incomplete thought that adds extra, non-essential information, you should use a comma to connect them. The phrase "making it one of the largest cities..." tells us more about the 20,000 inhabitants but isn't essential for the main sentence to make sense.

fd11f2cd-dabb-498a-8fa6-f54fba9dde76.key_insight: Use a comma to separate a complete thought from an incomplete thought that adds extra, descriptive information.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This creates a run-on sentence. Without any punctuation, the two parts are just smashed together, which makes it hard to read and grammatically incorrect.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: You can't use a period here because the part after the blank, 'Making it one of the largest cities in North America at the time,' isn't a complete sentence on its own. It needs to be attached to the main sentence.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to connect two complete thoughts that are closely related. Since 'making it one of the largest cities in North America at the time' is not a complete thought, a semicolon is incorrect here.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what comes after it.
steps.content: The blank is followed by the word "that." This "that" introduces a descriptive phrase that tells us more about the lightning strikes. It's not starting a new, separate thought.

steps.title: Check if the phrase after 'that' is essential.
steps.content: The phrase "that it has become known as 'Maracaibo’s Lighthouse'" is essential because it explains *why* the strikes are described as "so bright, so localized, and so dependable." Without this phrase, we wouldn't understand the full impact of these characteristics.

steps.title: Use no punctuation when a 'that' clause is essential.
steps.content: When a 'that' clause provides essential information that directly describes or limits the word right before it, you don't need any punctuation. It's like the 'that' clause is part of the description itself, not a separate thought.

04764fee-a85f-4107-bec0-ddacf39b7ba5.key_insight: If a 'that' clause gives essential information about the word right before it, don't use any punctuation (like a comma or semicolon) to separate them.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using a colon here would incorrectly suggest that a list or explanation is about to follow, but the 'that' clause is simply continuing the description of the lightning strikes, not introducing a new idea or list.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to connect two complete thoughts or to separate items in a complex list. Here, the phrase after the blank ('that it has become known...') is not a complete thought on its own, and it's not part of a list that needs semicolons for clarity. It's an essential descriptive clause.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: A comma is used to separate non-essential information or to connect certain types of clauses. However, the 'that' clause here is essential to understanding *why* the lightning is so special. Putting a comma before an essential 'that' clause would incorrectly separate it from the word it describes.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence before the blank: "Jamaican British artist Willard Wigan is known for his remarkable microsculptures." This is a complete thought – it could stand alone as a sentence. Now, let's look at what comes after the blank: "Creations so small that they are best viewed through a microscope, Wigan’s sculptures are made from tiny natural materials, such as spiderweb strands." This is also a complete thought. It describes the sculptures and could be its own sentence.

steps.title: Check if both sides are complete thoughts
steps.content: Since both parts – what comes before the blank and what comes after – are complete thoughts, we need strong punctuation to separate them. A period is a good way to do this, as it clearly marks the end of one sentence and the start of another.

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation
steps.content: Because we have two complete thoughts, a period is the correct choice to separate them. This creates two clear, grammatically correct sentences.

07ee54b1-ed9b-4dcc-8fb0-056adaea0549.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts (sentences) that can stand on their own, you need strong punctuation like a period or a semicolon to separate them. A comma alone isn't strong enough.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Putting "microsculptures creations" together without any punctuation creates a run-on sentence. It jams two complete thoughts together without a proper break, making it hard to read.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using a comma alone between two complete thoughts (like "microsculptures, creations") creates a comma splice. A comma isn't strong enough to separate two full sentences on its own.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using "microsculptures and creations" tries to connect the two parts with 'and', but it still results in a run-on sentence. 'And' can connect two complete thoughts, but it usually needs a comma before it when doing so, and even then, the structure here doesn't quite work to make it a single, grammatically sound sentence.

steps.title: Find the blank and the surrounding words
steps.content: First, let's look at the blank and the phrase right before it: "After pleading for years—to no effect—for the passage of key antidiscrimination legislation, ______ until their demands were addressed." The phrase before the blank describes an action: *pleading* for legislation. We need to figure out *who* was doing the pleading.

steps.title: Identify the doer of the action
steps.content: The introductory phrase "After pleading for years..." describes an action that someone performed. When a sentence starts with a descriptive phrase like this, the very next thing in the sentence (the subject) should be the person or thing that performed that action. In this case, who was pleading for years? The activists were.

steps.title: Match the doer to the subject
steps.content: Since the activists were the ones pleading, the subject of the main part of the sentence must be "the activists." Let's check the choices to see which one starts with "the activists" immediately after the comma.

highlights.text: increased pressure on lawmakers by staging a sit-in protest

steps.title: Confirm the best fit
steps.content: Choice D, "the activists increased pressure on lawmakers by staging a sit-in protest," correctly places "the activists" right after the descriptive phrase, making it clear that *they* were the ones who had been pleading. This makes the sentence flow logically and clearly.

highlights.text: the activists increased pressure on lawmakers by staging a sit-in protest

0b129012-6640-49e6-92cc-c865568fe326.key_insight: If a sentence starts with a descriptive phrase that tells you *who* or *what* did something, the very next word after that phrase (the subject) must be the person or thing that performed that action. Otherwise, it sounds like something else did it!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with "pressure on lawmakers." It sounds like the *pressure* was pleading for years, which doesn't make sense. Pressure can't plead.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with "a sit-in protest." It sounds like the *protest* was pleading for years, which also doesn't make sense. A protest is an event, not something that can plead.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with "lawmakers." While lawmakers *could* plead, the context of the first sentence clearly states that Kitty Cone and 150 other *disability rights activists* entered the building after pleading. So, it's the activists who were pleading, not the lawmakers.

steps.title: Look at the verbs around the blank
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what verbs are already in the sentence. This will help us figure out the right tense.

steps.title: Check the existing verb tenses
steps.content: The sentence says atoms "travel faster and faster" and "they are diverted." Both "travel" and "are diverted" are in the present tense. This tells us the sentence is describing a general process or habitual action, not something that happened in the past or will happen in the future.

steps.title: Match the tense for consistency
steps.content: To keep the sentence consistent, the verb in the blank should also be in the present tense. We need a verb that describes what happens when the atoms reach a certain energy level as part of this ongoing process.

0c21f6af-5370-4add-879b-3525aad4cd2f.key_insight: When a sentence describes a general process or habitual action, all the verbs describing that process should usually be in the same tense, typically the present tense.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using "will reach" puts the action in the future. But the rest of the sentence describes a general process using present tense verbs like "travel" and "are diverted." It makes the timing inconsistent.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using "had reached" puts the action in the past perfect tense. This doesn't fit with the present tense verbs "travel" and "are diverted," which describe an ongoing or general process. It sounds like the atoms reached the level long ago, which doesn't make sense in this context.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using "are reaching" is present progressive, meaning the action is happening right now. While it's present tense, it implies the action is currently in progress at this very moment, rather than being part of a general, repeated process, which is what the other verbs "travel" and "are diverted" suggest.

steps.title: Look at the sentence structure
steps.content: First, let's look at the whole sentence. We have 'American abstract artist Richard ______ his installations to make passersby keenly aware of how one’s movements are affected by the physical features of one’s environment, assembles large-scale steel plates into sculptures that dominate the outdoor spaces they occupy.' Notice the comma after 'environment' and then the verb 'assembles'. This tells us that 'assembles' is the main verb for Richard Serra.

steps.title: Identify the main action
steps.content: Since 'assembles' is already the main action Richard Serra does, the blank needs a word or phrase that describes *how* or *why* he assembles them, or adds extra information about him. It can't be another main verb.

steps.title: Choose the correct descriptive form
steps.content: We need something that acts like an adjective or an extra detail, not a second main verb. The word 'intending' (with a comma before it) works perfectly here. It describes Richard Serra's purpose without being a main verb itself, creating a descriptive phrase that fits between the subject ('Richard Serra') and the main verb ('assembles'). This structure, with commas around the descriptive phrase, is common for adding extra, non-essential information.

0da67ea5-4f1c-45a0-a98b-058de5d276de.key_insight: If a sentence already has a main verb for its subject, any additional action or description of that subject in the middle of the sentence should be in a non-verb form (like an -ing word or a descriptive phrase) and often set off by commas.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If we say 'Serra is intending,' we have two main verbs ('is intending' and 'assembles') for one subject ('Serra') without a connecting word. This makes the sentence grammatically incorrect because it tries to have two main actions without proper structure.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Putting 'Serra, intends' creates a similar problem to A. 'Intends' is a main verb, and 'assembles' is also a main verb. You can't have two main verbs like this for one subject without a conjunction (like 'and'). The comma after Serra also doesn't work with 'intends' as a main verb.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: If we just say 'Serra intends,' we again have two main verbs ('intends' and 'assembles') for one subject ('Serra'). This creates a run-on sentence structure where two main actions are just jammed together without a proper connection or punctuation.

steps.title: Look at the end of the sentence
steps.content: The blank is at the very end of the sentence. This means we need to decide on both the word order and the final punctuation mark.

steps.title: Identify the type of question
steps.content: The sentence starts by saying a team investigated 'how' something. This is an *indirect question*, not a direct one. An indirect question tells you what someone asked or investigated, but it doesn't ask the question itself. Direct questions usually have the verb before the subject (e.g., 'How *could their use* be regulated?'). Indirect questions keep the normal subject-verb order (e.g., 'how *their use could* be regulated').

highlights.text: The toxic nature of some of these materials recently led a team from the University of Sheffield to investigate how
could their use be better regulated ?
their use could be better regulated .

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation
steps.content: Since the sentence is making a statement about what the team investigated (it's not asking a question directly), it should end with a period, not a question mark. This is a common rule for indirect questions.

0e36ccb6-3942-491c-a4a5-899cf6825218.key_insight: When a sentence tells you *what* someone asked or investigated (an indirect question), it should end with a period and follow normal subject-verb order, not the inverted order of a direct question.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a question mark and the word order for a direct question ('could their use be regulated?'). But the sentence is stating what the team investigated, not asking a question directly, so it needs a period and normal word order.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses the correct word order for an indirect question ('their use could be regulated'), but it incorrectly ends with a question mark. Since the sentence is making a statement, it should end with a period.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses the word order for a direct question ('could their use be regulated?') even though the sentence is presenting an indirect question. It also uses a period, which would be correct if the word order were right, but the inverted word order makes it sound like a direct question that suddenly ends without a question mark.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, find the blank and see what's immediately around it. We have 'the plant’s ______ the cellular organs that generate energy from light—reshuffled'. Notice the dash after 'from light'. This is a big clue!

steps.title: Identify the extra information
steps.content: The phrase 'the cellular organs that generate energy from light' is extra information that defines 'chloroplasts'. It's like a little side note. When you have extra information that explains something, it often gets set off by punctuation. Since there's already a dash after 'from light', it tells us this extra information is being set off by a pair of dashes.

highlights.text: the cellular organs that generate energy from light

steps.title: Complete the pair of dashes
steps.content: Because the extra information 'the cellular organs that generate energy from light' is already closed by a dash, we need to open it with a matching dash. This creates a 'dash pair' to enclose the descriptive phrase. If you remove the phrase 'the cellular organs that generate energy from light', the sentence still makes sense: 'the plant’s chloroplasts reshuffled to form...'.

0f4f9a9e-e548-4685-8ff9-4a44b1f7f192.key_insight: When you see a dash setting off extra information in the middle of a sentence, look for another dash to complete the pair. This pair of dashes acts like parentheses, setting aside a descriptive phrase that could be removed without breaking the sentence.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Just putting 'chloroplasts' here leaves the extra information 'the cellular organs that generate energy from light' hanging without proper punctuation to set it apart. It makes the sentence confusing because it's not clear where the main sentence picks up again.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to connect two complete thoughts or to separate items in a complex list. Here, 'the cellular organs...' is not a complete thought, and it's not part of a list. Also, you can't pair a semicolon with a dash to set off extra information like this.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: While commas can set off extra information, you can't mix a comma with a dash to do it. If you were using commas, both sides would need to be commas. Using a comma here and a dash later is inconsistent and grammatically incorrect.

steps.title: Find the descriptive phrase and its subject
steps.content: First, look at the beginning of the sentence: "Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day." This phrase describes *who* knows this information. The blank comes right after this descriptive phrase, so the word immediately following the blank must be the subject that this phrase describes.

highlights.text: Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day,

steps.title: Identify who is doing the 'knowing'
steps.content: Ask yourself: Who is 'knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day'? Is it the moths? No, the moths are the *subject* of the theory, not the ones who know this scientific fact. It must be the researchers, Yash Sondhi and Samuel Fabian, who have this knowledge. Therefore, the subject immediately after the comma needs to be 'the researchers'.

highlights.text: Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day,

steps.title: Match the description to the correct subject
steps.content: The phrase "Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day" describes the researchers. So, the sentence needs to start with 'the researchers' right after the comma. This makes choice A the correct answer because it clearly states that 'the researchers theorize' after the descriptive phrase.

highlights.text: Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day,
the researchers theorize that moths, mistaking nighttime lights for the Sun, continually try to reorient their bodies while flying near such lights.

18bdcd6a-c5d4-4424-b608-dc65dec0651e.key_insight: When a sentence starts with a descriptive phrase ending in -ing or -ed, the word immediately after the comma must be the person or thing that the phrase is describing.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice says 'the researchers' theory is that moths...' This makes it sound like the *theory* is doing the 'knowing,' which doesn't make sense. A theory can't know things; people know things.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice says 'moths mistake nighttime lights...' This makes it sound like the *moths* are 'knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day,' which is illogical. The moths are the subject of the theory, not the ones who know the scientific fact.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Similar to choice C, this option also starts with 'moths continually try...' This incorrectly suggests that the *moths* are the ones 'knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day.' The researchers are the ones with that knowledge.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence up to the blank and then immediately after it. We have: "The Limón technique...is known for its emphasis on breath control and its interplay of weight and weightlessness" followed by "dancers may explore, for example, the moment of mid-air suspension at the top of a jump."

highlights.text: dancers may explore, for example, the moment of mid-air suspension at the top of a jump.

steps.title: Check if each side is a complete thought
steps.content:
Now, let's see if the part before the blank is a complete thought. "The Limón technique, developed by Mexican-born dancer and choreographer Jose Limón, is known for its emphasis on breath control and its interplay of weight and weightlessness" — Yes, that's a complete sentence on its own. It has a subject (The Limón technique) and a verb (is known). 

Next, let's look at the part after the blank: "dancers may explore, for example, the moment of mid-air suspension at the top of a jump." — This is also a complete thought. It has a subject (dancers) and a verb (may explore).

highlights.text: dancers may explore, for example, the moment of mid-air suspension at the top of a jump.

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation for two complete thoughts
steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts that are closely related, you can join them with a semicolon. A semicolon acts like a soft period, connecting two sentences that belong together thematically. Since both parts of the original sentence are complete thoughts, a semicolon is the correct way to connect them.

1a502ec7-e0fe-4d51-8404-ffa474912ebb.key_insight: If both sides of the punctuation are complete thoughts (meaning they could stand alone as sentences), you can use a period or a semicolon to connect them. A comma alone isn't strong enough!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you just put 'weightlessness' with no punctuation, you're smashing two complete thoughts together without anything to separate them. This creates a run-on sentence, which is a common grammar error.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Adding 'which' after 'weightlessness' doesn't work here. 'Which' usually introduces extra information about a noun, but it can't be used to connect two full, independent sentences like this. It makes the second part sound incomplete or awkwardly attached.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using only a comma to connect two complete thoughts creates a 'comma splice.' A comma isn't strong enough to join two full sentences by itself; it needs a connecting word like 'and,' 'but,' or 'or' to help it, or you need stronger punctuation like a semicolon or a period.

steps.title: Find the blank and look around it
steps.content: First, let's locate the blank and see what comes right before and after it. We need to complete the sentence: 'When a given industry—water and electricity are two well-known examples—carries high infrastructural start-up costs and other barriers that discourage competition, ______ of just one or two suppliers per municipality.' The blank needs a subject and a verb that makes sense with the rest of the sentence.

steps.title: Identify the subject
steps.content: The sentence starts by describing 'a given industry.' The part in dashes ('water and electricity are two well-known examples') is extra information. The main subject of the first part of the sentence is 'industry.' We need a pronoun that refers back to 'industry' and a verb that agrees with it.

highlights.text: carries high infrastructural start-up costs and other barriers that discourage competition,

steps.title: Match the pronoun and verb
steps.content: Since 'industry' is singular, we need a singular pronoun to refer to it. 'It' is the correct singular pronoun. The verb 'consists' also agrees with a singular subject. So, 'it often consists' correctly refers to 'industry' and makes the sentence grammatically sound.

1a8aae2e-94cb-48e9-825e-525e19ab002b.key_insight: Pronouns must agree in number (singular or plural) with the noun they refer to. If the noun is singular, use a singular pronoun.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using 'these' is incorrect because 'industry' is singular, but 'these' is a plural pronoun. It doesn't match the singular subject.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using 'they' is incorrect because 'industry' is singular, but 'they' is a plural pronoun. It doesn't match the singular subject.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: While 'this' is singular, it's often used as a demonstrative pronoun (pointing to something specific). In this context, 'this often consists' sounds a bit awkward and less clear than 'it often consists' when referring back to 'industry.' 'It' is the more natural and precise pronoun here.

steps.title: Identify the introductory phrase and what it describes
steps.content: First, look at the beginning of the sentence before the blank. You'll see the phrase "Based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state ruled by a king." This phrase describes *what* is based on those events. It's describing the play itself, the *Rabinal Achí*.

highlights.text: Based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state ruled by a king,

steps.title: Match the introductory phrase to its subject
steps.content: An introductory phrase like this needs to be immediately followed by the noun it's describing. Since the phrase describes the play *Rabinal Achí*, the very next word after the comma must be "Rabinal Achí."

highlights.text: Based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state ruled by a king,

steps.title: Check the rest of the sentence for logical flow
steps.content: Now, let's make sure the rest of the sentence makes sense. If we use choice A, the sentence reads: "Based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state ruled by a king, Rabinal Achí tells the story of K’iche’ Achí, a military leader who had once been an ally of the king but was later captured while leading an invading force against him." This flows logically and clearly states what the play is about.

highlights.text: had once been an ally of the king but was later captured while leading an invading force against him.

1bf2e737-6516-4fe5-b333-1b94a5694754.key_insight: When a descriptive phrase starts a sentence, the noun it describes must come immediately after the comma. This is called a dangling modifier if the noun isn't there!

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice places "K’iche’ Achí" immediately after the comma. But the introductory phrase describes the *drama* (Rabinal Achí), not the *character* (K’iche’ Achí). It would incorrectly suggest that K’iche’ Achí himself was based on those events, not the story about him.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice puts "the military leader" after the comma. The introductory phrase describes the *drama*, not a military leader. This creates a dangling modifier, making it seem like the military leader is 'based on events that occurred when Rabinal was a city-state ruled by a king,' which isn't the intended meaning.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with "there was a military leader." This is too wordy and doesn't directly link the introductory phrase to the subject it describes. The phrase "Based on events..." is describing the play, not the existence of a military leader.

steps.title: Find the subject of the sentence
steps.content: First, let's find the main thing the sentence is about. The blank is a verb, so we need to make sure it matches the subject. The subject of this sentence is "The vest frottoir."

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Now, let's figure out if "The vest frottoir" is one thing or more than one thing. Since it doesn't end in -s and refers to a single instrument, it's a singular subject.

steps.title: Choose the verb that matches the singular subject
steps.content: Since our subject, "The vest frottoir," is singular, we need a singular verb. Let's look at the choices. "Is" is a singular verb, while "have been," "were," and "are" are all plural.

1fc71343-03ef-4a67-8653-8022a0569f26.key_insight: A singular subject needs a singular verb, and a plural subject needs a plural verb. Pay close attention to whether the subject is one thing or many.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using "have been" would make the sentence sound like 'The vest frottoir have been,' which doesn't sound right because 'have been' is for plural subjects (like 'they have been').

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using "were" would make the sentence sound like 'The vest frottoir were,' which is incorrect because 'were' is a plural verb (like 'they were').

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using "are" would make the sentence sound like 'The vest frottoir are,' which is incorrect because 'are' is a plural verb (like 'they are').

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: The blank is in the middle of a sentence. We have 'carbon isotope,' before the blank and 'due to the higher' right after. The phrase 'carbon-13 (13C)' is extra information that describes the 'rare carbon isotope.'

steps.title: Identify extra information
steps.content: The phrase 'carbon-13 (13C)' gives more detail about the 'rare carbon isotope.' This kind of extra information, which isn't essential for the sentence to make sense, is called a non-essential clause or phrase. It needs to be set off by commas (or other punctuation like dashes or parentheses) on both sides.

steps.title: Use commas to set off the extra information
steps.content: Since 'carbon isotope,' already has a comma before the extra information, we need another comma after 'carbon-13 (13C)' to complete the pair. This shows that the information in between the commas could be removed without making the sentence grammatically incorrect.

264d3b92-3c6e-4dba-91e0-aff38c50100e.key_insight: When you have extra information in the middle of a sentence that isn't essential, set it off with a comma on both sides. If there's already a comma before it, you'll need one after it too!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'carbon-13' but then immediately opens parentheses. The comma isn't needed there because the parentheses already separate 'carbon-13' from '13C'. More importantly, it's missing the comma after the parenthetical information to close off the non-essential phrase.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice has no punctuation after 'carbon-13 (13C)'. Without a comma there, the extra information isn't properly set off from the rest of the sentence, making it sound like it's a necessary part of the sentence rather than an explanation.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice incorrectly places a comma after 'carbon-13' and before '(13C)'. The parentheses already separate 'carbon-13' from '13C', so an extra comma there is unnecessary and creates awkward punctuation. While it does have a comma after the parenthetical, the internal punctuation is incorrect.

steps.title: Identify the blank and what it refers to
steps.content: The blank is a pronoun, which means it needs to refer back to a noun mentioned earlier in the sentence. Let's look at what the Bishop condemned.

steps.title: Find the noun the pronoun replaces
steps.content: The sentence says, 'The Bishop of Ostia, St. Peter Damian, condemned the eating utensils because he considered ______ dangerous and unnecessary luxury items.' The blank refers to what the Bishop condemned: the 'eating utensils.'

steps.title: Match the pronoun to the noun
steps.content: Since 'utensils' is a plural noun (it ends in -s), the pronoun that replaces it must also be plural. The only plural option among the choices is 'them'.

26af4ca2-8099-499f-99b4-369ee610a483.key_insight: A pronoun must always match the noun it refers to in number (singular or plural). If the noun is plural, the pronoun must be plural.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: 'This' is a singular pronoun. It wouldn't make sense to say 'he considered this dangerous' when referring to multiple 'utensils'.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: 'That' is a singular pronoun. It doesn't match the plural noun 'utensils'.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: 'It' is a singular pronoun. You can't use 'it' to refer to more than one 'utensil'.

steps.title: Look at the sentence and the blank
steps.content: The sentence describes a tool and what it does: "This tool ______ economic potential, sustainability, and citizens’ quality of life." We need a verb that fits the subject 'This tool' and makes sense in the context of the paragraph.

steps.title: Check the surrounding sentences for clues
steps.content: The sentence before the blank says, "Economists in India, for example, use an Ease of Living Index." The word 'use' tells us that this tool is currently being used. The sentence with the blank describes what the tool *currently* does.

steps.title: Choose the verb that shows a current, general action
steps.content: Since the tool is currently in use and the sentence describes what it generally does, we need a verb in the simple present tense. The subject 'This tool' is singular, so the verb needs an '-s' at the end.

27505d92-da59-4abe-832b-227d0d3ea59a.key_insight: When describing a general fact or something that happens regularly in the present, use the simple present tense. Make sure the verb matches the subject (singular subjects often take verbs ending in '-s').

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'had measured' uses the past perfect tense, which suggests an action completed before another past action. This doesn't fit because the tool is currently 'used' (present tense) to measure things.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'would have measured' talks about something that would have happened in the past under different conditions. This doesn't make sense here because the tool is actively being used now.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'will have been measuring' uses the future perfect continuous tense, which describes an ongoing action that will be completed at some point in the future. This doesn't fit because the tool is currently performing this action.

steps.title: Look at the blank and the surrounding words
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what comes right before and after it. The sentence starts with "To survive when water is scarce, embryos inside African turquoise killifish eggs ______ a dormant state known as diapause."

highlights.text: embryos inside African turquoise killifish eggs
a dormant state known as diapause

steps.title: Identify the subject and what it needs to do
steps.content: The subject of this part of the sentence is "embryos inside African turquoise killifish eggs." We need a word that shows what these embryos *do*. They perform an action. This means we need a main verb that clearly states that action.

highlights.text: embryos inside African turquoise killifish eggs

steps.title: Choose the correct verb form
steps.content: We need a verb that directly tells us what the embryos do. "Enter" is a simple, direct verb that works perfectly here. It tells us that the embryos *perform* the action of entering a state. The other options are not main verbs; they are forms that can't stand alone as the primary action of the subject in this type of sentence.

2a6b69ca-d94c-4c1f-8fd7-593cad6ce6b5.key_insight: Every complete sentence needs a main verb that shows what the subject is doing. Forms like '-ing' words or 'to + verb' usually can't be the *only* main verb in a simple sentence.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'embryos to enter,' it doesn't sound like a complete action. It leaves you wondering, 'to enter what?' or 'what about entering?' It's not a complete thought on its own.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using 'having entered' makes the sentence sound incomplete. 'Embryos having entered' doesn't tell us what the embryos *do* right now; it describes something that happened before, but it's not the main action of the sentence.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'embryos entering,' it also sounds unfinished. 'Entering' is often used to describe something, like 'the embryos, entering the state, did X,' but it can't be the main verb that tells us what the embryos *do* in this sentence.

steps.title: Look for time clues in the sentence.
steps.content: First, read the sentence carefully and look for any words or phrases that tell you when the events are happening. This will help you figure out what verb tense to use.

highlights.text: Upon returning from the three-day excursion
for his remaining six years in office

steps.title: Check the tense of other verbs in the sentence.
steps.content: Notice that the sentence starts with 'In 1903' and describes events that already happened. The other verbs in the sentence, like 'guided' and 'upheld,' are also in the past tense. This tells you that the whole story is being told about past events.

steps.title: Choose the verb tense that matches.
steps.content: Since all the other time clues and verbs point to the past, the blank should also be filled with a past tense verb. 'Vowed' is the past tense form of 'vow,' which fits perfectly with the rest of the sentence.

2c077f09-1b16-4eea-bd6d-fa0a9eedd4a2.key_insight: When a sentence describes events that happened in the past, all the verbs telling that story should usually be in the past tense. Look for time words and other verbs to guide you!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using 'is vowing' (present progressive) makes it sound like Roosevelt is making the vow right now, which doesn't match the historical context of the sentence (1903).

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using 'will vow' (future tense) suggests Roosevelt is going to make the vow sometime in the future, but the sentence is clearly talking about something that already happened in 1903.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using 'vows' (simple present tense) would imply that Roosevelt makes this vow regularly or that it's a general truth, but the sentence is describing a specific event that occurred in the past.

steps.title: Look for the blank and surrounding words
steps.content: First, find the blank in the sentence. Then, read the words immediately before and after it to understand the context. The blank comes after "animal" and before "the just treatment of the elderly, and the abolition of the slave trade."

steps.title: Identify the sentence structure
steps.content: Notice that the sentence describes a list of things established by the Law of Piety: "the sanctity of animal life," "the just treatment of the elderly," and "the abolition of the slave trade." This is a list of three items.

highlights.text: the just treatment of the elderly,
and the abolition of the slave trade.

steps.title: Punctuate items in a list consistently
steps.content: When you have a list of three or more items, you use commas to separate each item. Since the second and third items in this list are already separated by a comma (before 'and'), you need to use a comma after 'life' to separate the first item from the second.

highlights.text: the just treatment of the elderly,

2febaf47-6724-42e3-a332-4dcd2ce3b3f8.key_insight: When listing three or more items, use commas to separate each item in the list. Make sure your punctuation is consistent throughout the list.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Leaving no punctuation after 'life' makes the sentence confusing because it doesn't clearly separate the first item in the list from the second. It makes 'animal life the just treatment' sound like one long, jumbled idea.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to separate complete thoughts or complex list items that already contain commas. Here, 'the sanctity of animal life' is not a complete thought on its own, and the other list items are separated by commas, so a semicolon would be inconsistent and incorrect.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: A colon is typically used to introduce a list or an explanation, not to separate items within a list. Using a colon here would incorrectly introduce 'the just treatment of the elderly' as if it were an explanation of 'animal life,' rather than another item in a series.

steps.title: Find the main action of the sentence
steps.content: Look at the sentence: "Some historians ______ that this 'tulip mania' was the first historical instance of an asset bubble..." We need a word that tells us what the historians *do* or *did*.

steps.title: Check if the sentence has a complete verb
steps.content: A complete sentence needs a main verb that shows the action. If we use 'claiming,' 'having claimed,' or 'to claim,' the sentence doesn't have a clear action performed by 'some historians.' It would sound incomplete, like 'Some historians claiming that...' without finishing the thought.

steps.title: Choose the verb that completes the thought
steps.content: The word 'claim' makes the sentence complete and grammatically correct: 'Some historians claim that this 'tulip mania' was the first historical instance of an asset bubble...' This tells us directly what the historians do.

327c93e5-4b23-48ee-b0ca-ee490bc67219.key_insight: Every complete sentence needs a main verb that clearly shows the action of the subject. Words ending in '-ing' or starting with 'to' (like 'claiming' or 'to claim') often don't act as the main verb unless there's a helping verb with them.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you use 'claiming,' the sentence becomes 'Some historians claiming that this tulip mania...' This sounds like an unfinished thought or a description, not a complete statement about what historians do.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using 'having claimed' also leaves the sentence incomplete. 'Some historians having claimed...' doesn't tell us what they *are doing* now or *did* as a main action; it just describes them as having done something in the past.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'to claim' is an infinitive, which means it shows purpose or potential but doesn't act as the main verb of the sentence. 'Some historians to claim...' doesn't make a complete statement about what historians do.

steps.title: Look for time clues in the sentence.
steps.content: First, read the whole sentence and pay close attention to any verbs or phrases that tell you *when* things are happening. This will help you figure out the correct tense for the blank.

steps.title: Identify the existing verb tenses.
steps.content: Notice the verb 'made' later in the sentence. This verb is in the past tense. Also, 'collected' is a past participle used to describe the data, which also points to a past event. This tells us that the action in the blank should also be in the past.

steps.title: Choose the verb that fits the timeline.
steps.content: Since Bonnie 'made' a discovery in the past, she must have been doing something else in the past at that same time. The phrase 'when she made an interesting discovery' suggests an ongoing action that was interrupted or accompanied by another past action. 'Was studying' (past progressive) correctly shows an action that was in progress in the past.

highlights.text: when she made an interesting discovery

35ccf6d1-35c2-40a6-bba0-e94d7ab85b2c.key_insight: When a sentence describes two past actions, and one was happening *while* the other occurred, use the past progressive tense (e.g., 'was studying') for the ongoing action and simple past for the completed action.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Choosing 'studies' (present tense) doesn't fit because the rest of the sentence talks about something that happened in the past ('made' a discovery, data 'collected'). The tenses need to match.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using 'has been studying' (present perfect progressive) suggests an action that started in the past and continues to the present. This doesn't match the clear past event signaled by 'made an interesting discovery'.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Selecting 'will study' (future tense) is incorrect because the sentence is clearly about a past event. The discovery 'made' by Bonnie Buratti already happened.

steps.title: Find the subject of the blank's verb
steps.content: First, let's figure out what the blank is describing. The blank comes right after the word "which." In this sentence, "which" refers to "the Nerf football." So, the verb in the blank needs to agree with "the Nerf football."

steps.title: Check if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Is "the Nerf football" singular or plural? It's just one football, so it's singular. This means the verb in the blank also needs to be singular.

steps.title: Match the verb and noun to the singular subject
steps.content: Now, let's look at the choices. We need a singular verb and a singular noun to describe "the Nerf football." Choice D, "is a smaller, foam version," uses the singular verb "is" and the singular noun "version." This matches our singular subject, "the Nerf football."

445a163e-b4fc-4a92-881d-1cb48f548323.key_insight: Make sure the verb and any related nouns agree in number (singular or plural) with the subject they are describing. If the subject is singular, the verb and noun should also be singular.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses "were," which is a plural verb. Since "the Nerf football" is singular, a plural verb doesn't make sense here.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses "are" (a plural verb) and "versions" (a plural noun). Both of these are plural, but "the Nerf football" is singular, so they don't match.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses "were" (a plural verb) and "versions" (a plural noun). Both are plural, but "the Nerf football" is singular, so they don't match.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence and see what comes right before and after the blank. We have 'overburdened national parks' before the blank and 'it prioritized physical improvements' immediately after.

steps.title: Check for complete thoughts
steps.content: Now, let's see if the part before the blank is a complete thought and if the part after the blank is a complete thought. A complete thought can stand alone as a sentence.

steps.title: Connect two complete thoughts
steps.content: Both parts are complete thoughts. 'The Mission 66 initiative...parks' can stand alone, and 'it prioritized...public' can also stand alone. When you have two complete thoughts that are closely related, you can connect them with a semicolon. A semicolon acts like a soft period, showing a close connection without fully separating them into two sentences.

45665d69-4ebd-4bba-8c24-cb8a56a26f20.key_insight: If both sides of the punctuation are complete thoughts (meaning they could each be their own sentence), you can use a period or a semicolon to connect them. You cannot use just a comma.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you use 'parks and', you're connecting two complete thoughts with 'and' but without a comma before 'and'. When connecting two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction (like 'and', 'but', 'or'), you need a comma before the conjunction.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Putting 'parks' directly next to 'it prioritized' creates a run-on sentence. You're smashing two complete thoughts together without any punctuation or connecting word, which makes it hard to read.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using just a comma after 'parks' creates a comma splice. A comma alone isn't strong enough to connect two complete thoughts; it needs a coordinating conjunction (like 'and', 'but', 'or') to help it, or you need stronger punctuation like a semicolon or period.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's look at the blank. We need to describe the 'political writings' of Thomas Paine. The sentence tells us that Paine moved to Paris, where *his* writings would contribute to the French Revolution. This means the blank needs to show possession (whose writings?) and describe the writings themselves.

steps.title: Determine possession for 'author'
steps.content: The 'writings' belong to a single author, Thomas Paine. To show that something belongs to one person, we use an apostrophe followed by an 's' (e.g., 'dog's bone'). So, we need 'author's' to show that the writings belong to the author.

steps.title: Determine the form of 'writings'
steps.content: The phrase 'political writings' refers to multiple works or pieces of writing. When we're talking about more than one, we use the plural form. So, 'writings' (without an apostrophe at the end) is correct here, as it's just a plural noun, not showing possession itself.

steps.title: Combine for the correct answer
steps.content: Putting it all together, we need 'author's' to show possession by a single author, and 'writings' to show that there are multiple works. This leads us to 'author's political writings'.

4a24e200-e984-41f9-a198-5b959f6d3314.key_insight: To show that something belongs to one person or thing, use 'apostrophe + s' (e.g., 'student's book'). To make a word plural (meaning more than one), just add 's' or 'es' (e.g., 'books', 'boxes')—don't add an apostrophe unless it's also showing possession.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'authors', which is plural but doesn't show possession. The writings belong to one author, Thomas Paine, so we need 'author's'.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'writing's'. While 'author's' is correct for possession, 'writing's' makes 'writing' possessive, but we need the plural form 'writings' to refer to multiple works, not something belonging to 'writing'.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'authors'' which implies multiple authors, but the sentence is about Thomas Paine, a single author. It also uses 'writings'', which incorrectly makes 'writings' possessive when it should just be a plural noun.

steps.title: Find the main subject and verb
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence: "However, yellow ______ considered complementary to blue in modern color theory." The subject of this part of the sentence is "yellow."

steps.title: Check if the sentence has a complete verb
steps.content: For a sentence to be complete, it needs a main verb that tells us what the subject is doing or being. The blank needs to provide that main verb for "yellow."

steps.title: Choose the correct verb form
steps.content: We need a verb that works with "yellow" to form a complete thought. "Is" is the correct form because "yellow is considered" makes a complete, grammatically correct sentence. It tells us what yellow 'is' in modern color theory.

53d723d9-878b-4d2d-8e20-0839ccf68813.key_insight: Every complete sentence needs a main verb that agrees with its subject and shows tense (past, present, future). If a sentence is missing this, it's a fragment.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: If you say "yellow having been considered," it doesn't form a complete sentence. It sounds like a phrase that needs more information to make sense, not a standalone statement.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using "yellow to be considered" also doesn't create a complete sentence. "To be" forms are often used for purposes or intentions, but they don't act as the main verb of a sentence on their own.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase "yellow being considered" is similar to B and C; it's a descriptive phrase, not a complete verb that can stand alone as the main action of the sentence. It leaves the sentence feeling unfinished.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what comes after it.
steps.content: The blank comes before the word "complexity." We need a word that shows possession – something *belongs* to the phrase. The sentence is talking about the complexity *of* the phrase. This means we need a possessive form of "phrase."

steps.title: Check the number of the noun.
steps.content: The sentence refers to a single phrase: "his famous phrase 'I think, therefore I am.'" Since it's one phrase, we need the singular possessive form, which is "phrase's." This rules out options that use a plural possessive like "phrases'."

steps.title: Match the pronoun to the noun.
steps.content: After the blank, the sentence continues: "masks its complexity." The word "its" refers back to the "phrase." Since "phrase" is singular, the possessive pronoun referring to it must also be singular. "Its" is the correct singular possessive pronoun. "Their" would be used for a plural noun.

55561358-f28b-4b75-bca1-71d0c6d16f0b.key_insight: When showing possession for a single item, use an apostrophe and an 's' (e.g., 'dog's'). Make sure any pronouns that refer to that item also match its singular or plural form.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'phrases'' which is the possessive form for multiple phrases. The sentence is only talking about one phrase, so this is incorrect.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'phrases' without an apostrophe, which is a plural noun, not a possessive one. It also uses 'their,' which is a plural pronoun, but the sentence is about a single phrase.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice correctly uses 'phrase's' for the singular possessive. However, it then uses 'their' to refer back to the phrase. Since 'phrase' is singular, it should be 'its,' not 'their.'

steps.title: Look for the comparison
steps.content: The sentence starts with a comparison: "Compared with that of a highly concentrated market." The word "that" here refers to the HHI score. So, we're comparing an HHI score to another HHI score. The blank needs to complete this comparison logically.

highlights.text: Compared with that of a highly concentrated market

steps.title: Identify what is being compared
steps.content: The first part of the comparison is "the HHI score of a highly concentrated market" (implied by "that of"). For the comparison to make sense, the second part, which comes after the blank, must also be an HHI score. We need to make sure the subject of the clause after the blank is what is actually being compared.

highlights.text: Compared with that of a highly concentrated market

steps.title: Match the subjects of the comparison
steps.content: Since the first part of the comparison is about an HHI score, the part after the blank must also logically refer to an HHI score. We are comparing two HHI scores. Choice B correctly makes "the HHI score of a less concentrated market" the subject, directly comparing it to the HHI score of a highly concentrated market.

highlights.text: Compared with that of a highly concentrated market
the HHI score of a less concentrated market will be much lower.

56fcac87-8717-435b-85b8-babcd6ffd2a7.key_insight: When you see a comparison, make sure you're comparing apples to apples! The thing being compared in the first part of the sentence must match the thing being compared in the second part.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice says "a market that is less concentrated will have a much lower HHI score." This incorrectly compares "a market" (the subject) to "that of a highly concentrated market" (which refers to an HHI score). You're comparing a market to an HHI score, which doesn't make sense.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice starts with "when a market is less concentrated." This creates a confusing sentence structure where the comparison isn't clear. It also makes the sentence sound awkward and less direct.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Similar to choice A, this choice says "a less concentrated market will have an HHI score that is much lower." This again compares "a less concentrated market" (the subject) to "that of a highly concentrated market" (an HHI score), which is an illogical comparison.

steps.title: Find the subject of the verb
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what word or phrase needs a verb. The blank is for a verb that describes what the 'various cultural and ideological frameworks' do. So, we need to figure out if 'frameworks' is singular or plural.

steps.title: Check if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: The word 'frameworks' ends in an 's', which means it's plural. This tells us that the verb we choose must also be plural to agree with it.

steps.title: Match the verb to the plural subject
steps.content: Since 'frameworks' is plural, we need a plural verb. In the present tense, plural verbs generally don't end in 's'. Let's look at the choices. 'Underlie' is the plural form that matches 'frameworks'.

5c087f74-469c-4bfc-b660-e7bc3cf611d6.key_insight: When a subject is plural (like 'frameworks'), its verb must also be plural (like 'underlie'). Singular verbs often end in 's' (like 'underlies'), while plural verbs usually don't.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you use 'underlies', it sounds like a single 'framework' is doing the action, but the sentence clearly talks about 'frameworks' (plural). So, 'underlies' doesn't match the plural subject.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using 'is underlying' makes the subject sound singular ('is' is for singular subjects), but 'frameworks' is plural. It also changes the tense slightly, making it continuous, which isn't the best fit here.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Similar to choice B, 'has been underlying' uses 'has', which is for singular subjects, not plural 'frameworks'. It also implies a continuous action that started in the past and continues, which isn't what the sentence is trying to convey about the general nature of frameworks.

steps.title: Look at the blank and the surrounding sentences
steps.content: First, read the sentences before and after the blank. The first two sentences describe how fast penguins launch themselves. The sentence immediately after the blank explains *how* they do it: "A layer of microbubbles on their plumage reduces friction as the penguins speed to the surface."

highlights.text: A layer of microbubbles on their plumage reduces friction as the penguins speed to the surface.

steps.title: Identify the purpose of the blanked sentence
steps.content: The sentence after the blank provides an *explanation*. This means the sentence in the blank should be asking a question that the next sentence answers. It should ask 'How do they do that?'

highlights.text: A layer of microbubbles on their plumage reduces friction as the penguins speed to the surface.

steps.title: Choose the correct question format and punctuation
steps.content: Since the blank needs to form a direct question, it should start with the helping verb ('are') before the subject ('they'). And, of course, a direct question needs a question mark at the end.

highlights.text: are they able to move so fast?

5c4f49f3-c040-46f8-8369-b9e615222cb3.key_insight: If the sentence after a blank answers a 'how' or 'why' question, the blank itself should be a direct question ending with a question mark, and the helping verb usually comes before the subject.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses an exclamation point, which implies strong emotion or surprise. While the speed is surprising, the next sentence *answers* a question, so the blank needs to *ask* one. Also, 'they are' is the order for a statement, not a direct question.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses the correct question structure ('are they'), but it ends with a period. A period is used for statements, not for direct questions. Since the next sentence answers the question, a question mark is needed.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice ends with a period and uses the word order 'they are,' which is for a statement. The sentence needs to be a direct question because the following sentence provides the answer.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence structure around the blank. We have 'Such interpretations are ultimately ______ the object’s gray coloration may be an incidental effect of radiation, solar wind, or collisions with other objects rather than evidence of its physical makeup.'

steps.title: Check if each side is a complete thought
steps.content: Let's see if the parts before and after the blank are complete thoughts. 'Such interpretations are ultimately speculative' is a complete thought. 'The object’s gray coloration may be an incidental effect of radiation, solar wind, or collisions with other objects rather than evidence of its physical makeup' is also a complete thought. Since we have two complete thoughts, we need strong punctuation to connect them.

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation for two complete thoughts
steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts, you can connect them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (like 'and', 'but', 'or'). Here, the word 'though' acts as a transition, showing a contrast. A semicolon is needed to properly separate the two complete thoughts, and a comma is used to set off 'though' as an introductory element to the second complete thought. So, ', though ;' works best.

5ce55e29-72c2-496c-a0f6-574f2e9874f4.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts, you need strong punctuation to connect them. A semicolon (;) is one way to do this, especially when a transitional word like 'though' introduces the second complete thought.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using just a comma before 'though' and then nothing to separate the two complete thoughts creates a run-on sentence. A comma alone isn't strong enough to connect two complete thoughts without a coordinating conjunction.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Placing the semicolon after 'speculative' and before 'though' incorrectly separates 'though' from the second complete thought it's meant to introduce. The semicolon should come after 'though' to connect the two complete thoughts, with a comma setting off 'though' itself.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using two commas (', though ,') to connect two complete thoughts is a comma splice. A comma splice is a common error where two complete thoughts are incorrectly joined by only a comma.

steps.title: Identify the introductory phrase
steps.content: First, look at the beginning of the sentence. We have the phrase "Supported by biochemical analyses of over 2,000 skeletons from the Middle Ages." This phrase describes *what* was supported by the analyses. We need the next part of the sentence to clearly state what that 'what' is.

highlights.text: Supported by biochemical analyses of over 2,000 skeletons from the Middle Ages,

steps.title: Check for a logical subject
steps.content: The introductory phrase describes something that was 'supported.' So, the word immediately following the comma must be the thing that was supported. Let's look at the choices to see which one logically fits.

steps.title: Match the subject to the introductory phrase
steps.content: The biochemical analyses *support* findings or a study, not vegetables, diets, or components directly. Choice D correctly places "findings from a 2022 study" right after the comma, making it clear that the findings are what were supported by the analyses.

highlights.text: Supported by biochemical analyses of over 2,000 skeletons from the Middle Ages,

5e70d6cc-7353-43f7-aa3d-bef448943e1a.key_insight: When a sentence starts with a descriptive phrase ending in a comma, the word right after the comma must be the thing being described. Make sure it makes logical sense!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice makes it sound like 'vegetables and grains' were supported by biochemical analyses, which doesn't make sense. The analyses support the *conclusions* about the vegetables and grains.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice suggests that 'early medieval rulers' diets' were supported by biochemical analyses. While the analyses *revealed* things about the diets, the diets themselves aren't 'supported' by the analyses in this context. The *findings* about the diets are what's supported.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice implies that 'the primary components' (vegetables and grains) were supported by biochemical analyses. Similar to A and B, this creates a confusing meaning because the analyses support the *conclusion* about the components, not the components themselves.

steps.title: Look at the verbs around the blank
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what kind of action it's describing. The sentence talks about what the Sherpas do when an eclipse is coming. We need to make sure the verb in the blank matches the timing of the other actions in the sentence.

steps.title: Check the tense of nearby verbs
steps.content: Read the sentence and pay close attention to the verbs that are already there. We see 'is' (as in 'is imminent') and 'pack' (as in 'pack up their telescopes'). Both of these verbs are in the present tense, describing ongoing or habitual actions.

steps.title: Match the tense for consistency
steps.content: Since the sentence is describing what the Sherpas *regularly do* when an eclipse is imminent, all the verbs should stay in the present tense to keep the sentence consistent. The blank needs a present tense verb to match 'is' and 'pack'.

60a5ca24-757a-4181-acca-0505c2ad7f0b.key_insight: Keep all verbs in a sentence in the same tense unless there's a specific reason to show a change in time (like something happened before something else).

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using 'had gotten' would put the action in the past perfect tense, suggesting it happened before another past event. This doesn't fit with the present tense verbs 'is' and 'pack' that describe what the Sherpas do regularly.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using 'got' would put the action in the simple past tense. This would make the sentence inconsistent because 'is' and 'pack' are in the present tense, describing a current or habitual action.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: Using 'were getting' would put the action in the past progressive tense, suggesting an ongoing action in the past. This doesn't match the present tense verbs 'is' and 'pack' that describe what the Sherpas do regularly.

steps.title: Look at the blank and the surrounding text.
steps.content: The blank is right after the word "nutrients." Let's read the whole sentence, paying close attention to the part before the blank and the part after it. The sentence starts with "Photosynthesis," and then there's a descriptive phrase: "the mechanism by which plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into nutrients." After this phrase, the sentence continues with "is fueled in part by an enzyme called Photosystem II..."

highlights.text: Photosynthesis, the mechanism by which plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into
is fueled in part by an enzyme called Photosystem II that harvests energy-giving electrons from water molecules.

steps.title: Identify the extra information.
steps.content: The phrase "the mechanism by which plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into nutrients" is extra information that describes photosynthesis. It's like a helpful side note. If you remove it, the main sentence still makes sense: "Photosynthesis is fueled in part by an enzyme called Photosystem II..."

highlights.text: is fueled in part by an enzyme called Photosystem II that harvests energy-giving electrons from water molecules.

steps.title: Use commas to set off extra information.
steps.content: When you have extra information like this in the middle of a sentence, you need to set it off with commas on both sides. Since there's already a comma after "Photosynthesis" to start this descriptive phrase, you need another comma after "nutrients" to close it off.

6383a60a-86d0-4f6d-8492-511f2e61978f.key_insight: If you have extra information in the middle of a sentence that could be removed without changing the main meaning, use a pair of commas to set it off.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Just saying 'nutrients' without a comma leaves the descriptive phrase hanging. It makes the sentence hard to read because the extra information isn't clearly separated from the main sentence.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Adding 'and' after 'nutrients' doesn't make sense here. 'And' is used to connect items in a list or two complete thoughts, but here we're trying to close off an extra descriptive phrase. It also doesn't provide the necessary punctuation to separate the extra information.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: While dashes can also set off extra information, you can't mix a comma at the beginning of the phrase ('Photosynthesis, the mechanism...') with a dash at the end ('...nutrients—'). You need consistent punctuation, so a comma pairs with a comma.

steps.title: Look for time clues in the sentence
steps.content: The first step is to read the sentence carefully and look for any words or phrases that tell you when things are happening. These are your time clues! In this sentence, we see a few important ones.

steps.title: Understand the sequence of events
steps.content: The sentence tells us the organization was formed in 1967. Then, it says that 'By the end of the 1990s,' something happened to its membership. This means the doubling happened sometime *before* or *during* the end of the 1990s, but *after* it was formed in 1967. Both of these time markers are in the past relative to now.

steps.title: Choose the correct past tense
steps.content: Since the doubling happened in the past (before the end of the 1990s), we need a past tense verb. 'Had doubled' is the past perfect tense, which is used to show an action that was completed before another point in the past. This fits perfectly because the doubling was completed by the end of the 1990s.

6cc3c0ee-cde2-4fdf-8b4b-3a8b2b247f84.key_insight: When a sentence describes an action that was completed before a specific point in the past, use the past perfect tense (had + past participle). Look for time markers like 'by the end of' or specific past dates.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: The present perfect 'has doubled' is used for actions that started in the past and continue to the present, or for actions completed in the recent past with a connection to the present. This doesn't fit because the sentence clearly places the doubling in a specific past period ('By the end of the 1990s').

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The present tense 'doubles' is used for actions happening now or for general truths. The sentence is talking about something that happened in the past, not something that is happening currently or generally.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The future tense 'will double' is used for actions that will happen in the future. The sentence is clearly discussing events that occurred in the past ('By the end of the 1990s').

steps.title: Look at the verb before the blank
steps.content: First, find the blank and look at the word right before it. The word is "decided." This verb often tells you what kind of word or phrase needs to follow it to complete its meaning.

steps.title: Consider what 'decided' needs
steps.content: When you 'decide' something, you usually decide *to do* something. For example, 'I decided to go to the store,' or 'She decided to study harder.' The verb 'decide' often pairs with the infinitive form (to + verb) to show the action that was decided upon.

steps.title: Choose the correct form
steps.content: Based on how 'decided' usually works, we need the 'to + verb' form. This means 'to include' is the best fit here. It clearly states what the Olympic committee decided to do.

6e2fc7f7-a36f-4729-871d-b8548dbc206e.key_insight: Many verbs pair with specific forms to complete their meaning. 'Decide' often takes the 'to + verb' (infinitive) form to show what action was chosen.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'decided included,' it sounds awkward and incomplete. 'Included' is a past tense verb, and you can't usually follow 'decided' directly with another past tense verb in this way to express the intended meaning.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using 'decided including' doesn't make sense in this context. 'Including' is usually used to list items or give examples, not to state the action that was decided upon. For example, 'The list included many sports, including tug-of-war.'

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: While 'include' is a verb, 'decided include' is grammatically incorrect. You can't directly follow 'decided' with the base form of a verb like this to show what was decided. It needs the 'to' before it.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what follows it
steps.content: The blank comes right before "chorus-to-verse ratios." This phrase tells us that the ratios belong to something. We need to figure out what that something is.

steps.title: Identify the relationship: possession
steps.content: The sentence says "chorus-to-verse ratios trended similarly, with *each genre's data* indicating..." This tells us that the ratios belong to individual genres. Since the blank is followed by "chorus-to-verse ratios," we need the possessive form of the genres mentioned.

steps.title: Choose the correct possessive form
steps.content: We need the possessive form for 'rock' and 'rap' because the ratios belong to these genres. The singular possessive is formed by adding an apostrophe and an 's' (e.g., 'rock's', 'rap's'). The sentence also mentions that "each genre's data" was considered, confirming that we're talking about the ratios of rock and the ratios of rap separately.

71b41422-0af5-443f-8f0d-e8268c6a91ba.key_insight: When something belongs to a singular noun, make it possessive by adding an apostrophe and an 's' (e.g., 'the dog's bone'). If you're talking about multiple things belonging to multiple singular items, each item needs its own possessive form.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'rocks' and 'raps,' which are plural nouns, not possessive. The ratios don't *are* rocks and raps; they *belong to* rock and rap.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'rocks' (plural) instead of 'rock's' (possessive). The ratios belong to 'rock,' not 'rocks.'

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'rock' (singular noun) instead of 'rock's' (possessive). It also implies a single ratio for 'rock and rap' combined, but the sentence specifies 'each genre's data,' meaning the ratios for rock and rap are considered individually.

steps.title: Find the subject of the sentence
steps.content: First, let's figure out who or what the sentence is about. The main subject here is "Farouk El-Baz." The phrase "a geologist and space scientist" just describes him.

steps.title: Check if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Is "Farouk El-Baz" one person or more than one person? Since it's one person, the subject is singular.

steps.title: Match the verb to the singular subject
steps.content: Now we need a verb that matches a singular subject. We're talking about something that happened in the past ("during the 1960s and 1970s"), so we need a past tense verb. The singular past tense form of 'to be' is 'was'.

7329735a-30da-41d5-a251-586ace0f8ef9.key_insight: A singular subject needs a singular verb. A plural subject needs a plural verb. Don't let extra descriptive words between the subject and verb trick you!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'are' is for plural subjects (like 'they are' or 'we are'), but 'Farouk El-Baz' is a single person. It also doesn't fit the past tense context of the sentence.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'have been' is for plural subjects (like 'they have been') or for 'I' or 'you'. 'Farouk El-Baz' is singular, and 'have been' doesn't fit the simple past tense needed here.

why_wrong.label: D
