why_wrong.reason: The verb 'were' is for plural subjects (like 'they were' or 'we were') or for 'you'. 'Farouk El-Baz' is a single person, so 'were' is incorrect.

steps.title: Identify the main list structure
steps.content: The sentence describes the materials Gavua uses. Look for the main items in this list. The sentence starts with 'Using natural debris, such as dried ______', then mentions 'such as plastic bags; and more traditional art supplies, such as tree glue'. This tells us there's a list of three main categories of materials.

highlights.text: Using natural debris, such as dried
such as plastic bags; and more traditional art supplies, such as tree glue

steps.title: Look for internal commas within list items
steps.content: Each item in the list itself contains a comma: 'natural debris, such as dried leaves' and 'man-made trash, such as plastic bags' and 'traditional art supplies, such as tree glue'. When the items in a list already have commas *inside* them, we use semicolons to separate the main list items to avoid confusion.

highlights.text: traditional art supplies, such as tree glue

steps.title: Apply semicolons to separate main list items
steps.content: Since the list items themselves contain commas (like 'natural debris, such as dried leaves'), we need to use semicolons to separate the main items in the list. The structure should be: Item 1; Item 2; and Item 3. This means we need a semicolon after 'leaves' and a comma after 'trash' to separate 'man-made trash' from its descriptive phrase 'such as plastic bags'.

highlights.text: such as plastic bags; and more traditional art supplies

7dbfce1a-5048-4658-8c7a-c6c89ab504a7.key_insight: When you have a list where each item already contains commas, use semicolons to separate the main items in the list to keep things clear.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'leaves', which doesn't match the semicolon used later in the list ('plastic bags; and more traditional art supplies'). All separators in a complex list should be consistent. Also, using a colon after 'trash' is incorrect; a colon usually introduces a list or explanation, not separates a noun from its descriptive phrase.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'leaves', which doesn't match the semicolon used later in the list ('plastic bags; and more traditional art supplies'). All separators in a complex list should be consistent. Also, using a comma after 'trash' is correct for separating 'man-made trash' from its descriptive phrase, but the initial comma after 'leaves' is the problem.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a semicolon after 'trash', which incorrectly separates 'man-made trash' from its descriptive phrase 'such as plastic bags'. You should use a comma there, not a semicolon, because 'such as plastic bags' is just extra information about 'man-made trash', not a separate complete thought.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence with the blank: "The vessel took six days to ______ it’s as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded." We need to figure out how to connect the idea of the vessel taking six days to dislodge with the information about its immense weight.

highlights.text: The vessel took six days to

steps.title: Check for complete thoughts
steps.content: Let's break down the sentence into parts. "The vessel took six days to dislodge, in part due to its sheer size" is a complete thought. It could stand alone as a sentence. "It’s as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded" is also a complete thought. Since we have two complete thoughts, we need strong punctuation to connect them.

steps.title: Choose the right punctuation
steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts, you can use a period, a semicolon, or a colon to connect them. A colon is a great choice here because the second complete thought explains or elaborates on the first one. The weight of the vessel (second thought) explains *why* it took so long to dislodge (first thought). Also, notice the phrase "in part due to its sheer size." This is extra information that describes *why* it took so long. It needs to be set off by a comma from the main part of the sentence.

highlights.text: dislodge, in part due to its sheer size:
in part due to its sheer size

81845f63-1dce-4263-98fd-e518dedab1ed.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts, and the second one explains or gives more detail about the first, a colon (:) is a perfect way to connect them. Remember to also use commas to set off extra information that isn't essential to the main idea of the sentence.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice doesn't use any punctuation to separate the phrase "in part due to its sheer size" from the rest of the sentence, which makes it a bit awkward. More importantly, it uses a comma to connect two complete thoughts ("The vessel took six days to dislodge in part due to its sheer size" and "it’s as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded"). You can't use just a comma to connect two complete thoughts; that's a comma splice.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice correctly uses a comma to set off "in part due to its sheer size." However, it then uses another comma to connect two complete thoughts ("The vessel took six days to dislodge, in part due to its sheer size" and "it’s as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded"). Again, you can't use just a comma to connect two complete thoughts; that's a comma splice.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses commas to set off "in part" and "due to its sheer size." While "in part" can sometimes be set off by commas, here it breaks up the phrase awkwardly. More critically, it leaves no punctuation at all between the two complete thoughts ("The vessel took six days to dislodge, in part, due to its sheer size" and "it’s as heavy as two thousand blue whales when fully loaded"). This creates a run-on sentence, which means two complete thoughts are just smashed together without proper connection.

steps.title: Find the main subject of the sentence
steps.content: First, let's figure out what the sentence is really about. The blank is part of the main verb. To pick the right verb, we need to find the main subject. Read the sentence carefully and ask yourself: what is 'limited to the realm of prose'? Is it Barbara Chase-Riboud herself, or something else?

steps.title: Identify if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: The sentence starts with 'The artistic talents'. Even though Barbara Chase-Riboud is mentioned, the actual subject performing the action (or not performing it, in this case) is 'talents'. Since 'talents' ends in an 's', it's a plural noun.

steps.title: Match the verb to the plural subject
steps.content:
Now that we know the subject 'talents' is plural, we need a plural verb to match it. Let's look at the choices:
*   'hasn't been' is singular.
*   'wasn't' is singular.
*   'isn't' is singular.
*   'aren't' is plural. This is the only verb that correctly matches the plural subject 'talents'.

8271fbab-f78b-4e48-ae7b-013af3917c6d.key_insight: Always make sure your verb agrees with its subject. If the subject is plural, the verb must also be plural. Don't get tricked by words that come between the subject and the verb!

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'hasn't been' is singular. It doesn't match the plural subject 'talents', making the sentence grammatically incorrect.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'wasn't' is singular. It doesn't match the plural subject 'talents', so the sentence would have a subject-verb agreement error.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The verb 'isn't' is singular. It doesn't match the plural subject 'talents', which creates a subject-verb agreement error.

steps.title: Look at what comes before and after the blank.
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence up to the blank: "In a 2016 study, Eastern Washington University psychologist Amani El-Alayli found that, among the study participants who experienced frisson (a physiological response akin to goosebumps or getting the chills) while listening to music, there was one personality trait that they scored particularly high." This part is a complete thought.

steps.title: Check the phrase after the blank.
steps.content: The phrase after the blank is "openness to experience." This phrase isn't a complete thought on its own. It's giving more specific information about the "personality trait" mentioned just before the blank.

steps.title: Choose the punctuation that introduces an explanation.
steps.content: Since the part before the blank is a complete thought, and the part after the blank explains or specifies something from the first part, a colon is the best choice. It clearly signals that what follows will clarify or list what was just mentioned. Also, the word "on" is needed to complete the phrase "scored particularly high on."

82ec50b7-22bf-4be1-a411-6f509b79115b.key_insight: Use a colon to introduce a list, an explanation, or a clarification that follows a complete thought.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Putting a period after 'high' creates a sentence fragment starting with 'On openness to experience.' This doesn't make sense as a separate sentence, and it separates 'on' from the verb 'scored high on' that it belongs with.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to connect two complete thoughts that are closely related. Here, 'openness to experience' is not a complete thought, so a semicolon isn't appropriate.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Just putting 'high on' with no punctuation doesn't clearly separate the complete thought from the specific trait being named. It makes the sentence a bit run-on and less clear about the relationship between the two parts.

steps.title: Find the subject of the verb
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what word needs a verb. The blank comes after 'tenth-century Japanese courtly life' and before 'readers a thousand years later.' The verb in the blank needs to describe what 'musings' do. The phrase 'on tenth-century Japanese courtly life' just describes the musings; it's not the subject.

steps.title: Check if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Now that we know the subject is 'musings,' we need to figure out if it's singular or plural. 'Musings' ends with an 's,' which tells us it's a plural noun. This means the verb we choose must also be plural.

steps.title: Match the verb to the plural subject
steps.content: Since 'musings' is plural, we need a plural verb. In the present tense, plural verbs (like 'fascinate') don't end in 's,' while singular verbs (like 'fascinates') do. 'Fascinate' is the correct plural form to match 'musings.'

8df0d88f-600a-480c-8f6d-0359367a3d4d.key_insight: When a subject is plural (like 'musings'), the present tense verb usually does NOT end in 's.' If the subject is singular (like 'a musing'), the present tense verb usually DOES end in 's.'

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'has fascinated,' which is a singular verb form. It would work if the subject was singular, like 'her book has fascinated,' but 'musings' is plural.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'fascinates,' which is a singular verb form (it ends in 's'). It doesn't match the plural subject 'musings.'

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'is fascinating,' which is a singular verb form. It doesn't agree with the plural subject 'musings.'

steps.title: Look at the blank and the surrounding sentence.
steps.content: The sentence starts with "Researchers Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley investigated how..." and then has a blank. The rest of the sentence continues, "In a series of experiments conducted in 2022, they found that people performing small acts of kindness underestimated the positive effect their actions had on others."

highlights.text: Researchers Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley investigated how

steps.title: Determine if the blank needs a direct question.
steps.content: The phrase "investigated how" introduces an indirect question, not a direct one. An indirect question is a statement about a question, not a question itself. For example, 'I wonder *what time it is*' is an indirect question, while '*What time is it?*' is a direct question.

steps.title: Choose the correct word order and punctuation for an indirect question.
steps.content: Because it's an indirect question, the word order should be like a statement (subject-verb), not a question (verb-subject). Also, since the entire sentence is a statement about what the researchers investigated, it should end with a period, not a question mark.

9c3dbaa0-1abe-4ecc-9ec1-086c55fad785.key_insight: When a sentence includes an indirect question (often introduced by words like 'how,' 'what,' 'where,' 'if,' or 'whether' after a verb like 'investigate,' 'ask,' 'wonder,' or 'know'), it should use statement word order (subject-verb) and end with a period, not a question mark.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses question word order ('do people perceive') which is incorrect for an indirect question. It also ends with a period, but the word order is the main issue.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses question word order ('do people perceive') and ends with a question mark. Both are incorrect for an indirect question within a statement.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses the correct statement word order ('people perceive') but incorrectly ends with a question mark. The sentence as a whole is a statement about what the researchers investigated, not a direct question.

steps.title: Look for time clues
steps.content: First, read the sentence carefully and look for any words or phrases that tell you when the action is happening or will happen. The blank is in the middle of the sentence, so check both sides.

steps.title: Identify the key time phrase
steps.content: The phrase 'in a later chapter' tells us that the learning will happen sometime in the future. This is a big clue about what verb tense we need.

steps.title: Match the verb tense to the time
steps.content: Since the learning will happen 'in a later chapter' (future), we need a verb that shows future tense. 'Will learn' is the correct future tense verb.

9f2a6225-1730-434c-b425-796f019b8180.key_insight: Always check for time clues in a sentence! Words like 'later,' 'next week,' or 'yesterday' tell you if an action is happening in the past, present, or future, which helps you pick the right verb tense.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'had learned,' it means the learning already happened in the past, before some other past event. But the sentence says 'in a later chapter,' pointing to the future.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Saying 'had been learning' also means the learning was happening in the past, over a period of time, before another past event. This doesn't fit with the idea of learning something 'in a later chapter' (future).

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: If you say 'have learned,' it means the learning started in the past and continues to the present, or it's a past action with a present result. This doesn't make sense with the phrase 'in a later chapter,' which clearly indicates a future event.

steps.title: Find the subject of the verb
steps.content: First, let's find the main subject of the sentence. The blank is part of the phrase "The radiation that ______ during the decay..." The word "that" refers back to "radiation." So, the verb in the blank needs to agree with "radiation."

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Is "radiation" singular or plural? "Radiation" is a singular noun. Think of it like "water" or "information" – it doesn't have a plural form in this context. Therefore, the verb that describes what the radiation does must also be singular.

steps.title: Choose the singular verb form
steps.content: Now we need to pick the verb that is singular and fits the sentence. For most verbs in the present tense, a singular subject takes a verb ending in -s (like 'he walks,' 'it runs'). The singular form of 'to occur' is 'occurs.'

a0080fdb-628f-467b-86e5-71a9c79a6243.key_insight: A singular subject needs a singular verb. In the present tense, singular verbs often end in -s (e.g., 'he walks,' 'it happens').

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The phrase "have occurred" is a plural verb form. Since "radiation" is singular, it doesn't match. You would say "they have occurred," not "it have occurred."

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The word "occur" is a plural verb form (like "they occur"). Since "radiation" is singular, it doesn't match. You wouldn't say "it occur."

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase "are occurring" is a plural verb form. Since "radiation" is singular, it doesn't match. You would say "they are occurring," not "it are occurring."

steps.title: Look for the main subject
steps.content: The sentence starts with a descriptive phrase: "Despite being cheap, versatile, and easy to produce." This phrase describes something. We need to make sure that the very next thing after the comma is the actual thing being described.

steps.content: The phrase "cheap, versatile, and easy to produce" is clearly talking about 'commercial plastics.' So, 'commercial plastics' should be the subject right after the comma.

steps.title: Connect the description to the subject
steps.content: Choice D correctly places 'commercial plastics' right after the comma, making it clear that the plastics are what's cheap, versatile, and easy to produce. The rest of the sentence then explains the problems with them.

a018db6b-acae-4258-860d-1734a7e3c85c.key_insight: When a sentence starts with a descriptive phrase followed by a comma, the word right after the comma must be the thing that the phrase is describing.

While 'commercial plastics' is in there, the main subject immediately following the comma is 'problems,' which creates the same illogical connection as choice B.

steps.title: Identify the main actions in the sentence
steps.content: First, let's figure out what Pura Belpré did. The sentence lists three main things she offered: storytelling, celebrating a holiday, and putting on puppet shows. These are parts of a list, and lists need careful punctuation.

steps.title: Look at the punctuation already in the list
steps.content: Notice how the last two items in the list are separated. We see a semicolon before 'and put on puppet shows'. This tells us that the list uses semicolons to separate its items, especially when the items themselves contain commas.

highlights.text: an important community holiday; and put on puppet shows

steps.title: Match the punctuation style
steps.content: Since the list already uses a semicolon to separate the second and third items, we need to use a semicolon to separate the first and second items as well. This keeps the punctuation consistent throughout the list.

steps.content: Also, consider the phrase 'an uncommon practice at the time'. The phrase 'at the time' directly describes 'practice' and is essential to its meaning here. We don't need a comma between 'practice' and 'at the time' because 'at the time' isn't extra, non-essential information.

a02d37da-76a6-44e5-a7c4-a5093f1ac51c.key_insight: When you have a list where some of the items already contain commas, use semicolons to separate the main items in that list. This helps keep the list clear and easy to read.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses a comma after 'practice' and then another comma after 'time'. The comma after 'practice' is unnecessary because 'at the time' is essential to describing the practice. The comma after 'time' is also incorrect because a comma isn't strong enough to separate items in a complex list that already has internal commas; a semicolon is needed here.

why_wrong.label: C

While it correctly doesn't put a comma after 'time', it uses a comma instead of a semicolon, which is needed to separate the main items in this complex list.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice correctly avoids a comma after 'practice', which is good. However, it uses a comma after 'time' instead of a semicolon. In a list where items themselves contain commas (like 'storytelling in both English and Spanish, an uncommon practice at the time'), you need semicolons to separate the main items for clarity.

steps.title: Look at the blank and its surroundings
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what words are right before and after it. We have "Generations of mystery and horror ______ have been influenced by the dark, gothic stories..."

steps.title: Identify the subject and verb
steps.content: The subject of the sentence is "Generations of mystery and horror writers." This whole phrase tells us *who* or *what* the sentence is about. The verb is "have been influenced," which tells us *what the subject does* or *what is done to it*. The blank is directly between the subject and the verb.

steps.title: Decide if punctuation is needed
steps.content: In standard English, you generally don't put punctuation directly between a subject and its main verb unless there's an interrupting phrase. Here, there's no interruption; the verb directly follows the subject. So, no punctuation is needed.

a2885835-97a1-4dd8-95e5-879e7fb317f3.key_insight: Don't put punctuation between a subject and its verb unless there's an interrupting phrase.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Adding a comma here would incorrectly separate the subject ('Generations of mystery and horror writers') from its verb ('have been influenced'). This creates an awkward pause where there shouldn't be one and is grammatically incorrect.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: An em dash (—) is used for emphasis or to set off an interrupting phrase. Here, there's no interruption or need for emphasis between the subject and its verb, so the dash is out of place.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon (;) is used to connect two complete thoughts or to separate items in a complex list. Here, we only have one complete thought, and the semicolon incorrectly breaks up the subject and verb of that single thought.

steps.title: Look at what's around the blank
steps.content: First, let's read the sentence carefully and see what comes right before and after the blank. We have: "Scientists had previously thought the Sun to be in a relatively 'quiet' phase at that [blank] the Lund team’s finding suggests otherwise."

steps.title: Check for complete thoughts
steps.content:
Now, let's see if the parts on each side of the blank are complete thoughts (sentences that can stand on their own). 

Before the blank: "Scientists had previously thought the Sun to be in a relatively 'quiet' phase at that time." This is a complete thought.

After the blank: "the Lund team’s finding suggests otherwise." This is also a complete thought.

Since both sides are complete thoughts, we need a way to connect them properly.

steps.title: Choose the right connector
steps.content: When you have two complete thoughts, you can connect them with a comma and a coordinating conjunction (like 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' 'so'). The word 'but' makes sense here because the second thought contrasts with the first one (scientists thought one thing, but the new finding suggests something different). So, a comma followed by 'but' is the correct way to join these two complete thoughts.

a3353019-ecb7-42cf-8c68-81297b37e992.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts that could be separate sentences, you can join them with a comma and a connecting word like 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' or 'so.' You can't just use a comma alone to connect two complete thoughts.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'but' to connect the two complete thoughts, which is good, but it's missing the comma before 'but.' When you connect two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction, you almost always need a comma before the conjunction.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses only a comma to connect two complete thoughts. This is called a comma splice, and it's a common grammar error. A single comma isn't strong enough to join two complete sentences on its own.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice has no punctuation or connecting word at all. This creates a run-on sentence, where two complete thoughts are just smashed together without anything to separate or connect them properly.

steps.title: Look for time clues in the sentence
steps.content: First, let's look at the sentence with the blank and the sentences around it. We need to figure out when this action is happening. The first sentence says, "Each night in Gijón, Spain, a section of the city’s marina is bathed in a soft green glow." The phrase "Each night" is a big clue!

steps.title: Match the verb tense to the time clue
steps.content: Since the glow happens "Each night," it's a regular, ongoing event. This means we need a verb that shows something happening habitually or generally true in the present. The verb "is bathed" in the first sentence is in the present tense, which matches this idea.

steps.title: Choose the present tense verb
steps.content: We need a verb for the blank that also shows a regular, present action. The subject is "A lamp," which is singular, so the verb needs to agree with it. "Illuminates" is a singular present tense verb that fits perfectly, showing that the lamp regularly lights up the glass.

highlights.text: A lamp inside the tree-shaped structure

steps.title: Connect two complete thoughts correctly
steps.content: Since we have two complete thoughts, we need a way to connect them properly. You can't just use a comma alone (that's a comma splice), or no punctuation at all (that's a run-on sentence). To connect two complete thoughts, you need either a period, a semicolon, or a comma followed by a connecting word like 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' etc. In this case, the second thought introduces a contrast or drawback to the first thought (synthetic fibers are durable, BUT they have a downside). So, a comma followed by 'but' is the perfect fit.

a7d3c869-3543-4a4e-bf30-3d5a33d72cc0.key_insight: If you have two complete thoughts that could stand alone as sentences, you need to connect them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma followed by a connecting word (like 'and,' 'but,' or 'or'). Don't just use a comma by itself!

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: While 'but' is the right connecting word, when you're joining two longer complete thoughts, it's standard to put a comma before the connecting word. Without the comma, it can feel a bit rushed or awkward.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Putting no punctuation or connecting word between two complete thoughts creates a 'run-on sentence.' It's like smashing two sentences together without any pause or connection, making it hard to read and understand.

why_wrong.reason: Using a dash after 'fast' and then another dash before 'during' creates confusion. Dashes are usually used in pairs to set off extra information within a single sentence, not to separate two complete sentences.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice creates a run-on sentence. It jams two complete thoughts together without any punctuation or connecting word, making it hard to read and understand where one idea ends and the next begins.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice creates a comma splice. A comma is not strong enough to separate two complete thoughts. Using only a comma here makes the sentence grammatically incorrect.

steps.title: Find the subject of the sentence
steps.content: First, let's figure out who or what is doing the action in this sentence. The blank is a verb, so we need to find its subject. Read the sentence carefully to identify the main noun that the verb needs to agree with.

steps.title: Check if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: The word 'speakers' ends with an 's', which tells us it's a plural noun. This means we need a verb that also matches a plural subject.

steps.title: Choose the verb that agrees with the plural subject
steps.content: Now we need to pick the verb form that works with a plural subject like 'speakers'. For most verbs in the present tense, a plural subject takes the base form of the verb (without an 's' at the end).

e30e121e-eb94-4a60-8a9f-349c35c37539.key_insight: A plural subject needs a plural verb. In the present tense, plural verbs usually don't end in 's' (e.g., 'they run,' not 'they runs').

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'is using' is a singular verb form. You would say 'he is using' or 'she is using,' but not 'speakers is using.' This doesn't match our plural subject 'speakers'.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: The word 'uses' is a singular verb form (e.g., 'he uses,' 'she uses'). Since our subject 'speakers' is plural, 'uses' doesn't fit.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: The phrase 'has used' is a singular verb form (e.g., 'he has used,' 'she has used'). It doesn't agree with the plural subject 'speakers'.

steps.title: Find the subject of the verb
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what word or phrase needs a verb. The blank comes right after "the country's name." This is what the verb needs to agree with.

steps.title: Determine if the subject is singular or plural
steps.content: Now, let's figure out if "the country's name" is singular or plural. "Name" is a singular noun, and it's not talking about multiple names. So, the subject is singular.

steps.title: Match the verb to the singular subject
steps.content: Since the subject "the country's name" is singular, we need a singular verb. Let's look at the choices. "Is" is a singular verb, while "are," "have been," and "are being" are plural.

e7ff466d-c81b-47b1-afb3-e8f157cfaaad.key_insight: Always make sure your verb matches its subject. If the subject is singular, the verb should be singular. If the subject is plural, the verb should be plural.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: Using "are" would make the sentence sound like there are multiple country names being pronounced, but the sentence is only talking about one name: "the country's name."

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: Using "have been" would also imply a plural subject, as if multiple names have been pronounced. The sentence refers to a single name, so this doesn't fit.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: Using "are being" is a plural verb form. It would incorrectly suggest that multiple names are currently being pronounced, rather than just one name.

steps.title: Look at the blank and what's around it
steps.content: First, let's find the blank and see what comes right before and after it. Before the blank, we have "mycology, the study of fungi". This phrase defines what mycology is. After the blank, we have "producing more than 350 paintings... and submitting her research...". This part describes *how* Beatrix Potter dedicated herself to mycology.

steps.title: Check if the parts are complete thoughts
steps.content: Let's see if the parts around the blank are complete thoughts. The main sentence is "Beatrix Potter is perhaps best known for writing and illustrating children's books... but she also dedicated herself to mycology, the study of fungi." The part after "fungi" is "producing more than 350 paintings..." This is not a complete thought on its own; it's a descriptive phrase telling us more about how she dedicated herself to mycology. It needs to connect smoothly to the rest of the sentence.

steps.title: Connect descriptive phrases with a comma
steps.content: Since "producing more than 350 paintings..." is a descriptive phrase that adds more information about Beatrix Potter's dedication to mycology, and it's not a complete thought, we need a comma to smoothly connect it to the preceding phrase. A comma is used to separate additional, non-essential information from the main part of the sentence.

edf05f38-94d8-41c7-9a60-581502e7cd50.key_insight: Use a comma to separate a descriptive phrase (like one starting with an -ing verb) that adds extra information but isn't a complete sentence on its own.

why_wrong.label: A
why_wrong.reason: A semicolon is used to connect two complete thoughts that are closely related, or to separate items in a complex list. Here, 'producing...' is not a complete thought, so a semicolon doesn't work.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: A period creates a new sentence. If we put a period here, 'Producing more than 350 paintings...' would be a sentence fragment because it doesn't have a subject performing the action.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: No punctuation here makes it sound like 'the study of fungi' is doing the 'producing' of paintings, which doesn't make sense. The sentence intends to say that Beatrix Potter was producing the paintings as part of her dedication to mycology.

steps.title: Identify the blank and surrounding words
steps.content: Look at the blank and the words right before and after it. We have 'butterfly flapping ______ in Brazil'. The blank needs to describe what the butterfly is flapping.

steps.title: Determine ownership and number
steps.content: The butterfly owns the wings, so we need a possessive form. Also, a butterfly has more than one wing, so we need the plural form of 'wing'.

steps.title: Choose the correct possessive and plural form
steps.content: The possessive form for 'it' (referring to the butterfly) is 'its' (no apostrophe). The plural form of 'wing' is 'wings'. So, we need 'its wings'.

ee1e31c1-0560-4c9c-a2fa-578ac6884e91.key_insight: Remember that 'its' (without an apostrophe) shows possession, like 'his' or 'her'. 'It's' (with an apostrophe) is a contraction for 'it is' or 'it has'.

why_wrong.label: B
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'wings'', which means 'belonging to the wings'. The wings don't own anything here; the butterfly owns the wings. We need the plural noun 'wings', not the possessive plural.

why_wrong.label: C
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'it's', which means 'it is' or 'it has'. We need the possessive form 'its'. It also uses 'wing's', which means 'belonging to one wing', but a butterfly has multiple wings, and we need the plural 'wings'.

why_wrong.label: D
why_wrong.reason: This choice uses 'it's', which means 'it is' or 'it has', instead of the possessive 'its'. It also uses 'wings'', which means 'belonging to the wings', but the wings don't own anything.
